comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints often speak of their own sins of youth out of moderation, and Job says this to match his friends' assumption.
comments.comment: … And if he speaks of his own 'sins of youth' and presents 'you have guarded all my works' as having sinned, it is not to be wondered at; for all the saints, for the sake of moderation and good-mindedness, offer such voices, just as the men in the furnace and the blessed David said: 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances' (Psalm 25:7). 'You have reached to the roots of my feet.' This means 'you have made all that concerns me as exact as the roots, that is, both the reasons and the beginnings of my practical progressions, to observe so that you might lead me to punishment.' And this again he says based on their assumption.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a righteous man like Job can speak of his own sins.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job describes decay only to answer the assumption that suffering proves sin.
comments.comment: He does not say these things of his own will, but in answer to what is being supposed, that everyone who is afflicted undergoes these things because he has sinned.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse is worded as it is in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job answers that a man born of woman is short-lived, so the weight of his trials cannot be put down to sin and are for a struggle.
comments.comment: He presents the cause of his suffering by joining together the weight of the temptation and human life; … he brings forward as a supporting argument for the matter not being so, 'but man born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath' (Job 14:1). Because of the hardship of life, he would not have brought such punishment upon the short-lived and full of wrath, unless he had encountered it for the sake of a struggle. For if the goodness of God and the brevity of men's lives had coincided, these things would not still have been reckoned as having happened because of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Job uses the brevity of man's life in his argument.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A passing man, like a flower and a shadow, was not struck with such evils because of sins, for if God marked iniquities none could stand.
comments.comment: That for the passing man, like a flower and a shadow, such evils were brought upon him, it is not according to the present context because of sins. 'For if he observes iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand? But with you is the atonement' (Psalm 130:3-4). So it was to be understood by the friends, that not because of mistakes, but as is foretold, because he was set before the goal of manliness, these things happened to him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Human life ends at the bound God appoints, which shows providence rather than chance or fate.
comments.comment:
Like a shadow, when he has passed through life, he leaves not even a memorial to the living.

Here he makes plain the providence over human beings: they do not stay in life at random or by chance, but by God's decree, and they do not pass beyond the life he has appointed. Yet these things must be said not as though fate were in control, but as though the will of God had arranged each thing by bounds and measures.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse as teaching God's ordered providence over the length of life.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God, who cares for men, would not demand justice from man so unyieldingly and absolutely as his friends suspected.
comments.comment: But indeed I have composed a discourse of this, not bypassing it so as to let it enter into judgment before you. A proof of this would be what is said toward God: 'My people, what have I done to you?' (Micah 6:3) and again, 'Behold, I am being judged against you.' For God, bringing in such a care concerning men, would not have demanded justice from man so unyieldingly and absolutely, as his friends suspected him of punishing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one is clean from filth, so Job shows he does not suffer for sin, since otherwise no one would be without trouble.
comments.comment: For who is clean from filth? Not even one, even if his life on the earth be but one day, and his months be numbered before you. And he joined these things together so that they might understand that he does not suffer because of sin. For if it were so, no one would be without trouble, even if he lived for a short time.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's argument from the universal filth of man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Filth and sin differ, since the filth is the unintentional acts which the Savior cleansed, as Isaiah says.
comments.comment:
And filth and sin, someone else might say, signify the same thing, with the one saying the filth of sin as something lesser of the other.

You have concerning filth and sin in Isaiah thus: 'The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and the daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst' (Isaiah 4:4), the blood signifying sin there, the unclean thing, and the filth the unintentional acts, which the Savior, having come, cleansed by himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man's span is shown to be set by God's judgment and will, not by fate or chance.
comments.comment: The providence concerning man is made clear here, not as if it remains in life as it happens and as it pleases, but from the judgment of God, not exceeding the time appointed by Him. And these things are not to be said as being held by fate, but as the will of God, 'having appointed each thing by limits and measures.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse about man's appointed bounds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A newborn, even if he lives only a day or a numbered few months, is not purified, because ignorance remains in one who begins to tell the false from the good.
comments.comment: And 'neither is the life of the one on earth even a single day' can be interpreted in two ways. There is the one being born now who has the sin of Adam by succession, … Nor will such a person be purified in a day, because ignorance remains for the one who has also begun now to distinguish the false from the good, even if he lives for a day, even if he lives for a numbered number of months.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Depart from Him' means 'cease your anger,' since under so many afflictions man would have no opportunity to repent.
comments.comment: Depart from Him, so that he may be at rest and find the life well-pleasing like the laborer. Since God is present to him through providences, the 'depart' has been said instead of 'cease your anger.' … For if he imposes such a multitude of afflictions upon him, man has no opportunity for repentance. He instructs them, therefore, that they do not understand this sensibly, through 'depart from Him, so that he may be at rest.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job would rather await his resurrection hidden in Hades than undergo so many pains, and the righteous before Christ's coming live better there.
comments.comment:
… being hidden there, 'until the wrath passes' (Job 14:13), as it is being said of God to remember him, in order to say more clearly that he would rather receive the time of his resurrection in Hades than undergo so many pains.

… the righteous man lives better during the time before the coming of Christ, since he is about to be liberated from the clamorous and sickly body to enjoy the incorruptible. … Not unsuitably, being persuaded and knowing concerning the resurrection of the dead, he places the more excellent deliverance from the painful life here, that it is more beautiful 'to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man's nature is not scattered like an animal's but immortal, so 'until I become again' signifies the resurrection.
comments.comment:
"If a man dies, he shall live having completed the days of his life" (Job 14:14), from which a doctrine concerning resurrection is presented and a judgment of each life in this life, not occurring randomly or by chance when death happens. …

… For the nature of man did not have it as they thought, that having possessed subsistence until the present life, having cast off this life, he is no longer, just like the irrational animals.

For the souls of irrational animals are scattered with their bodies, and therefore they are destroyed. But since the nature of man is not scattered, nor is he destroyed; for he is immortal. … "I will wait," for he says, "until I become again," signifying the resurrection
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the verse points to the resurrection and the immortal soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Until I become again' means resurrection is a kind of birth, in which the rising body is raised incorruptible.
comments.comment: The phrase 'until I become again' must be explained in this way: resurrection is a kind of birth. For this reason, 're-birth' is spoken in relation to the Savior. … Thus also of the resurrection, whether it is a transfer into the dust of the body, or into something else according to these changes, the rising body is raised incorruptible. It is, therefore, a birth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's call and Job's answer show that not only the body but also the soul is raised, so God does not cast away the works of his hands.
comments.comment:
But 'I will respond to you when you call again' stands in opposition to the opinion of those who mock: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa 22:13). …

Then 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' Wishing to show that not only the body is raised, but also the soul possessing the thoughts concerning God, he says, 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' For to listen to God calling is proper to a rational being. 'Do not cast away the works of your hands' (Job 14:15). Having taught concerning the resurrection of the whole human and the immortality of the soul, he instructs his friends so as not to consider him judged as insignificant by God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's call and answer as pointing to the resurrection of the whole man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job speaks as a sinner out of moderation and for his friends' instruction, so that they may imitate his words of repentance.
comments.comment: 'You have enumerated my faults to me, and you will not pass over any of my sins' (Job 14:16). … 'I will note if I have passed by unintentionally' (Job 14:17). As if speaking to them again, he says these things while they are at odds, as if he were undergoing these things as a sinner, and by moderation and for their instruction, so that they might imitate him being so pure and bringing forth words of repentance. 'You have sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Job 14:17). That is to say: 'You have included in them both the quality and the number.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rock seems unshakeable, but the falling mountain and aging rock show that whatever rises through pride or hardness will be condemned.
comments.comment:
And the rock is mentioned because it sends out the impression as unshakeable, and because Christ is being formed and is an imitator of the true rock, concerning which it was said: 'And the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). …

… And even after saying that 'you sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Job 14:17) and how regarding his own sin he had brought forward the previously set forth things, he applied the words 'but the mountain falling shall fall, and the rock shall be made old from its place' (Job 14:18) to show that 'even if a mountain arises through pride or through hardness, its condemnation shall be,' having perceived this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Water smooths stones as repentance frees a man of sin's roughness, so hope in man must not be lost, though without God his endurance is vain.
comments.comment:
Waters smoothed the stones, and waters overwhelmed the depths of the earth's soil; and did you destroy the endurance of man? He confirms through these things the previously spoken, that repentance is powerful.

For through 'waters smoothed the stones' (Job 14:19), he demonstrates that the one beginning to repent, persisting in this, according to the water which removes the excess from the stone, frees himself from the superfluities of sin, as if no longer having the roughness from it, and just as lying in the depths of soils, he works the flood of sin. 'If these things have this manner, do not recognize the endurance of man, nor say that this is destroyed when it has worn him down and gone to an end.' He moves the word toward God. For after saying that repentance is possible and that one must not lose hope in man, he brings the 'having worn him down and gone to an end' as an instruction, that unless God is a co-worker, the things of endurance are in vain. …

For unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it (Ps 127:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God turns his face away not from the worthy but from the sinner who thinks himself hidden, though God fills heaven and earth.
comments.comment:
God does not push away the worthy person, but the one positioned in such a way, saying: 'Depart from me, workers of iniquity, I never knew you' (Matt 7:23). He turns His face away and drives them out.

It is said: 'The face of the Lord is against those doing evil' (Psalm 34:16); and again the saints pray: 'Let your face shine and we shall be saved' (Psalm 80:3); and in others: 'May His face shine upon you and give you peace' (Num 6:25). Therefore, if the sinner, through God's great patience, remains unfeeling toward his failings, not thinking himself to be God, but desiring to remain hidden, saying: 'Darkness covers me from every side and the walls, who sees me?', God says: 'I am a God drawing near and not a God far off. Shall anyone hide in secret and I shall not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord' (Jer 23:24).

Having turned His face from the sinner, He sends him away, instead of 'showing him to be a stranger to Himself,' according to: 'God will drive them away because they did not listen to Him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Hosea 9:17) and: 'Like wounded women cast down sleeping in a grave, of whom you no longer remembered, and they themselves were driven from your hand' (Psalm 88:5). And though many of His sons became so, he did not know; even if a few became so, he does not know.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God changes his countenance and sends the sinner away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who falls under wrath suffers and mourns without knowing why, while the brave man bears hardships looking to the crown.
comments.comment:
Rather, his flesh grieved and his soul mourned. This shows that as the wrath against the sinner moves according to the secret words of providence, the one falling into it suffers and mourns, but is ignorant of the words of the handing over. These things are instructional, so as not to say to friends that they know that one suffers through sin.

For the one who does not endure suffers and is consumed when he falls into calamities, but the brave man, even if he is stung by hardships, bears them courageously toward the goal, looking away (Heb 12:2). For only the one who seeks nothing good or useful suffers if he is afflicted. But the virtuous man, like a crowned athlete, does not regard the hardships because of the expectation of the crown.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's pain of flesh and mourning of soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker begins foolishly, charging Job with empty, profitless words that come from the pains he cannot restrain.
comments.comment: Existing in a state of delusion and thinking that he suffers through sin, he begins his words by asserting that it is wise to answer with understanding, implying that Job does not answer with understanding. This one, then, is a fool, and he is striking at the holy man regarding his lack of understanding. And he filled his belly with toil by reproving with words that are not to be used, and in words that have no profit. As it has been said, he begins foolishly; for he says that it is wise of the wise to answer sensibly, but 'he filled his belly with toil by reproving with words that are not to be used,' instead of saying 'from the pains, which he had in his heart and is unable to restrain, he brings forth words that are not to be used, and words in which there is no profit,' scattering his words as if they were useless and futile things sent forth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The accuser, thinking Job suffers for sin, counts his bold words before the Lord as blasphemy and as proof against himself.
comments.comment: 'Will you not also cease from fear?' The preceding things are confirmed; for he reproves him as one who has not had fear, and it is clear that he also, by subjecting God, claims that because he has not had fear, but has suffered these things through sins, and that one not having fear uses such words. For they thought him bold, not knowing his virtue, supposing that having renounced fear, he says these things. 'Have you completed such words before the Lord?' Perhaps because of the easy availability of the words, which he brought forth purely from the one having conscience, he says these things, which this accuser considers as blasphemy, assuming the false beginning that he suffers through sin. 'You are guilty of the words of your mouth.' He dialogues with him with boldness as if he were bringing forth words against one who is not righteous. And he also thinks that he reproves him from his own words, asserting that 'you shall be reproved by words from yourself' (Job 15:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They tell Job he does not differ from other men and has no more grasp of the truth than they do.
comments.comment: For what? Did you not first come from men, or did you come upon the earth before the dusts? They want to present to him that 'you do not differ from other men, nor do you exist outside of their nature so as to have grasped more than the others,' in order that they might present themselves as having reached the truth, for which he suffers a cause.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The question asks whether Job was born before all men and lived long enough to gain more experience than others.
comments.comment:
“What then? Were you born the first of men? Or were you set fast before the dunes? Or have you heard the Lord’s ordinance?” (Job 15:7-8). That is: Did you come into being before all men, and, having stretched out your life until now, gain experience of more things than those of your own kind?

Theodotion: where the place is high and hard to cross, or sandy. The Hebrew has “you were conceived.” …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eliphaz denies Job any special wisdom, though he himself, not knowing God's judgment, should not have pre-judged Job a sinner.
comments.comment:
Or have you heard a divine arrangement, yet wisdom has come to you? Proposing the unsearchable nature of judgments from this, he thinks he is wandering into not knowing, that he suffers through something other than sin, being held by this. For he himself was not one having heard a divine arrangement or having wisdom come to him, so as to have a dispute concerning the Holy One as one suffering through sin. For what do you know that we do not know, or what do you understand that we do not? (Job 15:9).

He makes it common to all men, as if he were ignorant of the greatness of his virtue, and from this, as it is foretold, he is apparently overturning the idea of himself being righteous; which it was necessary that he, even while ignorant, should not pre-judge the judgment and be persuaded that he is bowed down as a sinner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The charge that Job knows more than they do is spoken from arrogant authority, and falsehood may come from honest error or from arrogance.
comments.comment:
"an elder," he says, "you are, and an old one among us, becoming more weighty than even your father"—instead of "more venerable"—"knowing more than we do." And he says these things from an arrogant authority.

… "A few of your sins have been scourged." He says this meaning: "You have sinned and because of this you undergo lashes. But since, enduring this, you add injustice to God, your sin has become more weighty." And he says these things not with understanding; for he did not know the matter as it was, so that he was speaking falsely. And there are various ways of being false. For there is a way of lying that is not malicious; for often we hold an opinion about something as being such and we say it, having the intention of speaking the truth, yet that which is reported is false by its own nature, but it is not said by one who is lying. And there is also the case of one who, not knowing anything at all, brings forth a false word out of arrogance, which is what happened to him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They took Job's bold words, which came from a pure conscience, for arrogance, in vain and without understanding.
comments.comment: "What did your heart dare, or what did your eyes lift up?" (Job 15:12). And they held these opinions about him, both hearing of his sins and because of his words of boldness. Since the blessed one brought forth words from purity, they thought this was an excess of arrogance, in vain and without understanding. "That you have broken a heart before the Lord, and have brought forth from your mouth such words."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those without virtue think it too hard for anyone to be blameless, yet Scripture speaks of man both as weak and as crowned with glory.
comments.comment:
For what mortal is there that will be blameless, or that, as he is to come, will be a righteous offspring of a woman? It is a characteristic of those who do not possess virtue to consider this undertaking difficult and to place it as if no one possessed it, just as the one before says, stumbling because of the body's nature as it is likely to be weak.

If he had observed according to the soul and according to the intellect, he contemplated the greatness of human nature, which the hymnographer teaches on both sides, saying: 'What is man, that you take thought of him? Man is made like vanity' (Psalm 144:3-4), which he has said regarding the weakness of the body as comparing it to divine things. But instructing on greatness, he says again: 'You made him a little less than the angels, you crowned him with glory and honor' (Psalm 8:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To 'believe' often means to be certain, and the 'heaven' not pure before God is the fallen angels, whose sword of punishment is drunken.
comments.comment:
He does not believe according to the saints. Similar to this is the 'if he does not believe according to his children, he thought something crooked concerning his angels.' Thus, there he says the angels are the saints, presenting that 'if even angels are corruptible, how can a man be blameless?' It should be noted that to believe often signifies the certain, as it is said: 'All his commandments are faithful' (Psalm 111:7). And he interprets their faithfulness saying: 'established unto the age of ages.' And again: 'the word is faithful and worthy of all acceptance.' And again: 'God is faithful and there is no injustice.' For God is not faithful from participating in faith, but from having certainty. And heaven is not pure before him.

Just as even the stars will not be compared to God's light, being without any darkness, and the heaven itself is not pure, not at all, but rather in addition to God. And it is possible to call these ones who 'left the heavenly dwelling' heaven here, whom he said 'his children, concerning whom he does not believe.' For God himself says in Isaiah from his own person: 'My sword is drunken in heaven' (Isaiah 34:5). And the sword signifies punishment, as it is said: 'My sword shall eat blood of wounds, and my arrows shall be drunken with blood' (Deuteronomy 32:42). Thus, among the angels who have fallen, he says the sword becomes drunken, bringing punishment called heavens. Therefore, this heaven is not pure before him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even a ruler who acts arrogantly has only a numbered span of years and carries fear of death in his ears, while the diligent man, knowing it is better to be with Christ, is hopeful.
comments.comment:
The Lord, commanding his own disciples, says: 'Do not worry about tomorrow' (Matt 6:34). And it is a command, so that 'we should throw all anxiety upon the Lord' (1 Pet 5:7). And if he also says that life is 'in care,' and that years are a numbered amount given to a ruler, then his fear is in his ears. This he says, that even if someone is a ruler and acts insolently, let him know that he has a numbered number of years.

Power does not make him long-lived; for time is measured for men by God toward His own judgment. Therefore, even if the ruler acts arrogantly, his life and his years turn out to be few, and he always has fear in his ears because of the uncertainty of the manner of death. Such a person has a fearful nature. For when he is in care regarding life, he reveres even death. But the diligent one, knowing that it is better 'to depart and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), is hopeful, not being such as the wicked, but one who fears; for it has been said that 'the impious flees when no one pursues' (Prov 28:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the wicked man seems at peace in his wealth, his destruction comes, as it did to the rich man in the Gospel.
comments.comment: When it seems to him that he is already at peace, his destruction will come. Even if someone exists in great prosperity, like the one saying in the Gospel: 'I will pull down my barns and build greater, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things, eat, drink, rejoice' (Luke 12:18-19); but the Lord says to him: 'Fool, this very night they will demand your soul from you; and what you have prepared, to whom will it belong?' (Luke 12:20). For when it seemed to him to be at peace in wealth, his destruction came.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse with the Gospel parable of the rich man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner's sudden destruction is like the pangs of a woman in labor, since he has stored up for himself punishments of iron and gypsum.
comments.comment: The phrase 'when it seems to him to be at peace, his destruction will come' is similar to 'when they say: It is peace and security' (1 Thess 5:3). He says, 'Then, sudden destruction stands upon them just like the pangs of a woman in labor.' For he has already been committed into hands of iron, and has been arranged into pits of gypsum (Job 15:22b–23a). For the one sinning has hoarded for himself punishments, which will come through iron and gypsum.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The conscience of sinners knows it remains in a state of falling, and necessity and tribulation will cast down the evil one as a leading general.
comments.comment:
He knows in himself, as in Job 15:23b, that he remains in a state of falling. He says that the conscience of those committing sin knows the expectation of the habits of the wicked, that this is a state of falling.

A day of darkness shall surround him (Job 15:23c), instead of 'he is being tossed about by afflictions.' You have in Amos concerning this day: 'Woe to those who desire the day, and why is this day of the Lord upon you? And this is darkness and not light' (Amos 5:18–20), 'and a gloom where there is no light' (Amos 5:20). This is also in Job 10:22a. Necessity and tribulation shall cast him down (Job 15:24a). He says, therefore, that the wicked will fall into these things, preparing for all evil, because through sin he suffers these things (Job 15:24b), like a leading general falling. Even if it is not Job who is saying these things, but he possessed some knowledge of the devil, which it is likely he obtained from the words of Job or from other ancients. He calls him a leading general because of his primordial wickedness. He says, therefore, that necessity and tribulation, as mentioned in the preceding things, shall cast him down in such a way as a leading general; thus he too shall fall, being primordially wicked.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked man is bold in evil as if his thick shield made him invincible, and like false prophets in sheep's skin he deceives by disguise.
comments.comment:
Insolence ran against him (Job 15:26a). It is manifest through the fact that he does not act in secret, but against the Lord. And insolence can be both arrogance and every injustice; for those being reproached makes them worthy of insolence. The one insulting someone says these words and calls them wicked. But he does not entirely make him worthy of insolence; for neither praise makes one good, nor reproach makes one bad. He is in the thickness of his shield. Because he is bold in evil, he shows this in this: for as he uses the shield as if invincible, through its thickness and through fleshly habits. So also the false prophets, having put on the skin of a sheep, were 'wolves snatching' from within.

… Being transformed into an angel of light, he deceives and snatches away, and not as the devil; for if he were openly so, we would have fled him. So also the prostitute, personified in the poems, injects the venom with goodly words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evil enters 'uninhabited houses', the souls from which every virtue, God and the Holy Spirit have departed, and finds no place where a great dwelling stands.
comments.comment:
But he enters into uninhabited houses.

These things seem to be said about the devil, or about every evil and opposing power and soul partaking of the same wickedness; for their receptive qualities are of the same kind. And if anything is said about the devil as evil, as a worker of evil, it is possible for this same wickedness to be said about another evil power. Therefore, in general, we say about every evil that it enters into uninhabited houses; for where there is a significant dwelling, the evil one has no place.

And we have from the Gospel to demonstrate this: 'When the unclean spirit,' he says, 'goes out from the man, it passes through dry places seeking rest and does not find it' (Matthew 12:43). But dry places in these matters are the souls that are destitute of wickedness.

… Therefore, the souls there are 'uninhabited houses,' from which every virtue has been separated, and in the absence of which God has departed, and His word and the Holy Spirit; into which the devil, the opposing power, enters.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked prepare evil through malice and pleasures.
comments.comment: And pay attention, that he did not say 'what they have done', but 'what they have prepared', and they prepared through malice, through pleasures, through other evils.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked man will not be enriched, and since he is not from the beginning and malice will not last, he casts no shadow on the earth.
comments.comment:
Neither shall he be enriched, nor shall his existing things remain with him.

… Similar to this is 'the partridge has hatched what she did not lay; at the end of it they will leave it, at the end of it it will be a fool' (Jeremiah 17:11). It will not cast a shadow upon the earth. Bodies are the makers of shadows, and it is impossible for a shadow to exist without a body. And this one, since having undergone a certain way, does not remain—I do not say that his essence does not remain, but that he does not remain as he wished to be—therefore he does not cast a shadow; 'for he was not from the beginning' (Wisdom 14:13), he says, and malice 'will not be unto the age' (Job 15:35).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Malice is not essential but enters from outside, so when temptation strikes like a wind it withers, as a physician cuts away a tumor to bring health.
comments.comment: Nor shall he escape the darkness. And rightly so; for the one who is an instigator for others toward malice receives an irrecoverable punishment. A wind withers his sprout. Even if it seemed to flourish in those whom he deceived and in those in whom he would fulfill his malice, but this sprout is withered by the wind; for he does not have a root. For malice is not essential, but entering from without, which, when struck by temptation, which is called wind, is rebuked and falls and withers. And his flower will fall. The flower is the beginning and the precursor of fruit, and this therefore falls. Even if the one participating in malice boasts, a little later he is humbled. And this is often even beneficial, just as a physician often cuts away the tumor attached to the body with iron and does not cease to apply painful things, until he fulfills the goal, the healthy state.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who pervert God's judgments fall under punishment.
comments.comment: Judgment will come against the gifted. Because 'the judgment of God is present' (Rom 2:5), those who pervert the judgments of God fall under punishments. And in the belly, pains shall be taken. He means this: the man becomes a father of ill-born ones, being the cause of punishments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His labors are filled with futility and his belly with deceit, which Scripture uses as a name for all wickedness.
comments.comment:
It will depart from him empty, and his belly will be filled with deceit. All his efforts, as it is foretold, are filled with futility, … And deceit here he says is all manner of wickedness.

For deceit is indeed a kind of wickedness, and nothing less, and all wickedness is called by the name according to what has been said: 'O full of all deceit and all trickery' (Acts 13:10) and 'therefore laying aside all deceit and hypocrisy' (1 Peter 2:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends accuse those in distress without distinction, so 'all' may mean all who misjudge suffering, or the three, whose number makes a multitude.
comments.comment: … since they bring their accusations to those in distress without distinction, as if to separate them as bad ones, it is appropriate—just as the three friends have done—that he brought the phrase 'all are accusers of evils,' meaning that all, through ignorance of what is happening differently than it ought, either raise up or contract the painful things; or he said 'all' regarding the three, for from this number comes the multitude.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Had Job stayed silent he would have been judged more unjustly, as if conscious of the charges.
comments.comment: 'And if I keep silent, how much less shall I be wounded?' 'And if indeed in silence,' he says, 'I were to contain the insults, I would not only fail to attain the glory of philosophy, but on the contrary, I would be judged much more unlawfully for the silence of one thought to be conscious of the things being said.' He had not previously done this, but it happened because the adversary requested it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job could not keep silent and why he was misjudged.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job asks the earth not to hide his blood and desires his cry to reach heaven so God may show that his life has been blameless.
comments.comment:
At a loss, he [Job] speaks to the earth, and calling it to sympathy he says words that are spoken as a wish. He says: Do not keep silent, O earth, about what has befallen me, and do not help to hide the blood unjustly poured from my flesh through my sores. Let it not stand still in one place and be hidden, and let my laments not pass into forgetfulness. Rather, he says, let many be built up through my trials. Or: let the earth not hide my blood but call God out to vengeance, with the very discharges of my body as its witnesses.

And may the air not hold back my cry, but may the force of my voice reach to heaven, so that God, standing up as avenger of the evils being done and punishing those responsible, may in this way at least show all people that my life has been blameless. The words “Behold, my witness is in heaven” belong to a most pure conscience.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the plea to earth and heaven means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Heavy words weary the soul like heavy loads weary beasts, and enduring insult belongs to a great man.
comments.comment:
“How long will you make my soul weary?” (Job 19:2). Just as heavy loads laid on the bodies of animals make the beasts that carry them weary, so there are some heavy words, and whoever hears them grows weary. As if pressed down by a weight — the force of the words spoken not well, but harshly or in abuse, by the other two who had come with Baldad, like the feeling of a heavy load — Job, weary in soul at what they had said, says: “How long will you make my soul weary?”

… You see how the sovereign of the Sauchaeans was described beforehand. His words are tyrannical, and when Job hears them he says: “How long will you make my soul weary?” Nothing reaches a man’s soul as a hard word does. Often someone who has endured tortures applied to his body has not endured words. The perfect athlete, though, even when he is weary, still endures harsh words; for to endure insult belongs to a great man. That is why the Apostle, among his own deeds of courage, says: “Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we bear it; being slandered, we entreat. We have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, until now” (1 Corinthians 4:12-13).

… Do you see? It is Job, whose book contains nothing so especially as his courage and his endurance. And yet he feels the weariness he had suffered from the hard word of those who had come to visit him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who see God afflicting Job should feel fear and pity rather than shamelessly reproaching him, even supposing he had sinned.
comments.comment:
“Only know that the Lord has done this to me” (Job 19:3). What you see in my case, do not think it has come to me from anywhere but from God. Be afraid, then; for he who brings these things on me can bring them on you as well.

“You speak against me; without shame before me you press upon me” (Job 19:3). Often a person even speaks against another and does wrong in it. But when he feels no shame, he says it to the other man’s face, not to correct him or to tell the truth, but to reproach and insult him. For one must not trample on those who are being punished by God, but lament and be afraid.

“Yes, truly I have gone astray, and a deceiver lodges with me, so that I speak a word I ought not” (Job 19:4). Then he [Job] speaks by way of supposition: I grant you, as you assume, that I suffer these things because of my sins; ought you then to reproach me like this? “And a deceiver lodges with me.” Even if, for argument’s sake, I had done such things as I ought not, even if I was that kind of man, ought you not, seeing the scourges, the running sores, the worms, the loss of my possessions, to have felt some respect? Instead you trample on me further, with no pity for me and no sympathy for my plight.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job’s friends trample him while God hems him in, and he meets their reproach by laughing and keeping silence, in the spirit of overcoming evil with good.
comments.comment:
“But let it be that you magnify yourselves against me and leap on me with reproach” (Job 19:5). You reproach me beyond measure; you leap on me, as if stepping on me and trampling me down, as you reproach me.

“And he [God] has raised his stronghold against me” (Job 19:6). It is as if I am under a wall: the stronghold of my plight, which I cannot escape until God decides to pull it down.

“Behold, I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak” (Job 19:7). This is the saying: “Overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

… Look, at your reproach I am thought to laugh, not to speak.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture often calls the body skin, and Job spoke of his own body when he said that his skin would be raised.
comments.comment: But that in many of the divine teachings the body is called skin, it is possible to find. For the blessed Job says: 'For I know that he who is about to release me is ever-enduring; he will raise my skin upon the earth that draws these things' (Job 19:26), and Job clearly spoke these things about his own body. And again the same says such things about himself: 'You clothed me with skin and flesh, and you brought me together with bones and sinews' (Job 10:11). For it is a clear and most evident sign that the skin garments are the body, since Job also remembers the one who clothed, which was also said concerning the first-formed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job means by his 'skin'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though the ungodly man's lofty prayers and sacrifices appear to reach heaven, he perishes utterly and vanishes like an empty dream.
comments.comment:
“If his gifts go up to heaven, and his sacrifice touches the clouds” (Job 20:6). This is the ungodly man: even if his gifts go up to heaven, even if he is lifted up very high, even if his sacrifice touches the clouds. Whenever the heretic prays, whenever his sacrifice goes up on the strength of his lofty talk, whenever he seems to have been set firm, then he will perish utterly. For his prayer is reckoned to him as sin, and his prayer itself is sin.

“For when he seems already to have been made firm, then he will perish utterly” (Job 20:7). It is like this saying: “But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they are glorified and exalted, vanish away like smoke” (Psalm 37:20).

“And those who have seen him will say: Where is he?” (Job 20:7). Who are the ones who have seen him? We of the Church, who have seen the errors of those men, will say: Where is he?

“Like a dream that has flown away, he will not be found” (Job 20:8). People of this kind dream and fashion phantoms for themselves. Because they have gone astray, they do not rest their mind on the truth, and they become like a dream that has flown away and will not be found.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The deeds of the ungodly teacher kindle his punishment, while the gall of an asp in his belly signifies doctrines opposed to the truth.
comments.comment:
“May the lesser ones destroy his sons” (Job 20:10). His sons: that is, the sons and disciples of the man who taught these things. “And may his hands kindle pains” (Job 20:10). His hands, he says, that is, his deeds, will kindle punishment for him.

“And his hands”: the hands of this ungodly and erring man, whose prayer is reckoned as sin, whose sacrifice may go up to heaven and touch the clouds, and then he perishes utterly. This man's hands will kindle pains; that is, they too will pass their days in the utmost pains. He is speaking about the sons of the lawless man.

“The gall of an asp is in his belly” (Job 20:14). For he holds teachings that are not sweet but are the gall of an asp: something wicked, as it were, the gall that belongs to the wine of their teaching. “For their vine is of the vine of Sodom” (Deuteronomy 32:32), and so on.

… The gall of an asp is in the belly of the man who holds other doctrines and is ungodly in his teachings, those that are opposed to the truth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God will not allow the fallen to retain their unjustly gathered words, nor will they share in the pasture of the good Shepherd.
comments.comment:
“Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited up” (Job 20:15). For what other wealth is gathered unjustly than the wealth that lies in their words? It is gathered unjustly. But the Good One will not allow them, fallen as they are, to keep the wealth gathered unjustly within themselves for ever; he will make them vomit it up.

“An angel will drag him out of his house” (Job 20:15). For an angel, by the working and the kindness of God, will drag him out of that very house which was badly built, which is a congregation of evildoers. That is his house. But an angel will drag him out of his house.

“May he not see the milking of the grazing flocks” (Job 20:17). The man who holds other doctrines does not see the milking of the grazing flocks. The grazing flocks are certain souls that feed under the good Shepherd, who said: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and go out and find pasture” (John 10:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Doctrines set against God yield no sweetness or profit, and worldly possessions cannot save a person from divine wrath and distress.
comments.comment:
“Like a tough herb that cannot be chewed or swallowed” (Job 20:18). The words and doctrines that are set against God are tough and dense; there is nothing sweet in them. The strifnos is a plant that turns rough on the tongue of the one who chews it. So, he says, just as no one can swallow that plant, however hard he strives to grind it down with his teeth, so too the man who wants to enjoy what belongs to others will carry off no profit from all his labors.

“Therefore his good things will not blossom” (Job 20:21). The things he seems to do as good will not blossom; “when he seems already to have been filled, he will be afflicted” (Job 20:22). “There is no salvation for him in his possessions” (Job 20:20). His possessions cannot win salvation for him.

… “And every distress will come upon him, and he will send upon him the fury of wrath” (Job 20:22-23). “And every distress will come upon him” (Job 20:22). These words urge us to keep away from what belongs to others.

“May he snow pains upon him” (Job 20:23). Instead of snow, pains come upon a man of this kind.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The iron represents a word that cuts most keenly.
comments.comment: “And he will not be saved from the hand of iron” (Job 20:24). By iron he does not mean the iron our senses perceive, but a word that cuts most keenly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fire that devours the ungodly is an invisible, internal punishment that burns like a severe fever.
comments.comment:
“And may an arrow pass right through his body” (Job 20:25). These fiery arrows wound him.

“A fire that no one kindled will devour him” (Job 20:26). We are learning a mystery about the punishment that is laid up, so that we may guard against suffering it. He said that an unkindled fire will devour the ungodly man. This material fire that we have is not an unkindled fire, for it is seen. But that fire which comes upon sinners is invisible, and it burns them within. It is a fire of the mind, and it punishes. If you want to take an image of that fire, think, I ask you, of someone with a raging fever, burning as if with fire. You will not find the fire in him by looking; yet it lies beneath and burns up his inward parts. In the same way a person who is feverish from his sins is burned up.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the unkindled fire means by comparing it to an inward fever.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The newcomer refers to the invader who destroyed the sanctuary and holy city.
comments.comment: “And may a newcomer ruin his house” (Job 20:26). The one who made war on that people was a newcomer and not a proselyte. He ruined his house, pulling down what was held to be a sanctuary and the city they called holy.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The unkindled fire signifies either the fire of conscience or future punishment, leaving the sinner unburied.
comments.comment: “An unkindled fire will devour him” (Job 20:26). In the hidden sense, the unkindled fire is either the fire of conscience, or else the fire laid up in the places of punishment to come. And he will be consumed as by fire, he says, meaning: he is not even thought worthy of burial.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The title Overseer belongs to God, whom faithful church leaders strive to imitate as living images.
comments.comment:
“And may heaven uncover his lawless deeds” (Job 20:27). That is: he will suffer terrible things both from God and from heaven. He said this because Job, after saying that he had been struck by God, also recalled that he had been wronged by men. So he argues that everything was brought upon him through sin. “And may the earth rise up against him” (Job 20:27). The earth itself rises up against that people.

“And a possession of goods is his from the Overseer” (Job 20:29). Learn who is named overseer here: God is called Overseer, and the overseers of the Church, the good and noble among them, strive in every way to bear his image. And just as the man who has copied a royal image is honoured for copying it well, and honoured too for having adorned it, so blessed is the overseer who has understood the true Overseer, who is zealous to be like him and becomes as God among men; or who has as his overseer the One who makes him truly an overseer in Christ Jesus. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job tells his friends that they claim to understand his suffering and condemn him as a sinner.
comments.comment: “Look at me and be amazed” (Job 21:5). You claim to be wise and to know why I suffer these things, on the ground that God does not sleep over the sins of men. And you have dared to say that I am a sinner and have come to this justly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By asking why the impious prosper, Job seeks the causes that God gives for what happens to men.
comments.comment: And he does the same in other matters, asking again: 'Why do the impious live, having been prospered even in wealth, their seed according to the soul, and their cattle not having failed to calve?' In order that he might also instruct through these, he seeks the existing causes from God of the things happening to men, which are secondary and pleasant.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The impious grow ever richer, beget a lesser seed according to the soul rather than the spirit, and do their works to be seen.
comments.comment:
“And they have grown old in wealth” (Job 21:7). They are not newly rich; they have spent many years being rich and always adding to their wealth.

“Their seed is according to the soul” (Job 21:8). The righteous man's seed is according to the spirit: for he sows to the spirit, and “of the spirit reaps eternal life” (Galatians 6:8). But with people of this kind, since “the man of soul does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14), the seed is not according to the spirit but according to the soul, the lesser part.

“And their children are before their eyes” (Job 21:8). Everything they do, they do “to be seen by men” (Matthew 23:5). For each person's works are his children. The children of those who hold other doctrines are not in the heart, in good thoughts, but before the eyes, to be seen by men.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Their assemblies prosper without fear of God or chastisement, and they bring their wicked conceptions to term.
comments.comment:
“Their houses prosper” (Job 21:9). When you go into an assembly of heretics and see a crowd gathered there, see how their houses prosper. “And there is no fear anywhere” (Job 21:9). They are without fear. They do not fear God; they despise the Godhead. Saying such things about God, they are not afraid, though it is about God that they are speaking. “And there is no scourge from the Lord upon them” (Job 21:9).

… If you see a man saying such things against God who is healthy in body, who sees, who keeps his senses whole, and who at times even seems to do well in the affairs of this world, see how in him, ungodly as he is, the words have been fulfilled: “And there is no scourge from the Lord upon them.”

“Their cow did not cast her calf” (Job 21:10). … The ox is a farming animal and works together with men at farming. They too farm. But what they farm is Sodom and Gomorrah; they farm Egypt. “Their cow did not cast her calf”: rather, she too brought forth and bore young, so that their wicked land might be farmed.

“And their pregnant one came safely through, and did not miscarry” (Job 21:10). Whatever they conceive, they also carry to term; they do not conceive from the fear of God but from wickedness. “Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived trouble, and gave birth to lawlessness” (Psalm 7:14).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The everlasting sheep are those who hear Christ's voice and receive eternal life.
comments.comment: “And they remain like everlasting sheep” (Job 21:11). What is the meaning of “they will remain like everlasting sheep”? These are the ones of whom Christ says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27-28), and so on. These are the everlasting sheep. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Rivals ape Christ’s church order and only seem like everlasting sheep, while their followers mock the Old Testament instead of praising God.
comments.comment:
… they imitate the everlasting sheep and so fulfil the words: “They remain like everlasting sheep” (Job 21:11). But they are not everlasting sheep; they only remain like everlasting sheep.

“And their children make sport” (Job 21:11). “Taking up psaltery and harp” (Job 21:12). Our people take up psaltery and harp to sing hymns to God and give him glory. But the children of those men, senseless as they are within themselves, make sport as they take up psaltery and harp. Whenever they take up the words of the Old Testament, they make sport of them and laugh at the oracles of the Law and the Prophets. They take up the instruments that are in tune, the psaltery of the Law and the harp of prophecy, and make sport with them.
comments.selected_reason: Once the opening is repaired, it plainly ties Job 21:11–12 to hypocrites who imitate the church’s order and misuse Scripture and music—readable against the wicked’s prosperity in context.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They rejoice in their own psalms and fall asleep in the rest of Hades rather than in God's rest.
comments.comment:
“And they rejoice at the sound of a psalm” (Job 21:12). They too recite psalms, the psalms of Valentinus, and recite odes, the odes of Basilides, and they utter things of that kind, rejoicing at the sound of a psalm.

“And in the rest of Hades they fell asleep” (Job 21:13). In rest, yes, but not the rest of heaven: it was in the rest of Hades that they fell asleep. But we pray to fall asleep not in the rest of Hades but in the rest of God, in the holy heavens, with Christ reigning over us. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The impious man, prospering, speaks to the Lord as if his prosperity came from nothing and he need not serve him.
comments.comment: From this audacity the impious man, prospering in finding what he desires, utters a voice like that in Job (Job 21:14-15): 'Depart from me, I do not wish to know your ways; what is sufficient, what shall we serve him?' For indeed they do not think the prosperity coming to them is due to anything, saying to the Lord: 'Depart; do not make your ways manifest to me; for I do not wish to know them; for what more is of us sufficient, that we may serve you?'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words of the prosperous impious man in verses 14-15.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only God truly teaches virtue, and the friends' words were recorded so readers may profit by testing them.
comments.comment:
“Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” (Job 22:2). What the Holy Spirit arranges must be counted worthy of being written down. That is why it is written: so that the reader may profit from what he reads. … One may, then, profit from his words by looking closely at the doctrines, and see that what is blameworthy in the words concerns one thing only: they blame Job, thinking that he suffers because of the sins he has committed, and they do not see that there are many other causes of what happens to people. …

The doctrine is sound: a human being cannot be a true teacher of virtue. … God teaches by shining into the soul of the one who learns from him and by lighting up his mind with the light, his true Word. So righteous men too teach us, when they have received the grace of teaching.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means about God as teacher in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God in kindness reproves those he cares for and allows them to speak as if he were on trial with them.
comments.comment: “And he will enter into judgement with you” (Job 22:4). God, taking account of the one he cares for, reproves him. … that God loves mankind so much that, even as he judges us kindly, he allows us to speak to him about whatever we wish, as though he were on trial with us. So I used the words of Isaiah: “Come, and let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:18). For “let us reason together” means something like this: If you have any charge to bring against me and my providence, as though I had neglected you, as though I had not done what was needed, speak. And I will say whatever I have to say, and I will persuade you, condemning you as one who deserves to be condemned.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording about entering into judgment as God's kindness in answering.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wickedness is the bad state of the soul, and its countless sinful acts explain great suffering.
comments.comment: “Is not your wickedness great, and your sins without number?” (Job 22:5). With reason, then, I say that you have not simply become unjust, since you suffer such things as none of the wicked suffer, but that you were born in these things; plainly, you have had more wickedness than the others among the wicked. Wickedness is a bad state in the soul, as of grief or of anger, and unseemly desire; sin is its activity. That is why he named wickedness first and then sin, calling the one great and the others numberless. … For it is likely that these things have come upon you because of your numberless sins and the multitude of your stumbles.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording about wickedness and sins in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eliphaz supposes Job's great sufferings must come from countless sins beginning with pledges taken for nothing.
comments.comment:
“Is not your wickedness great?” (Job 22:5). With good reason, I say, you have not simply been unjust; for he suffers things such as none of them has fallen into, things as great as yours. It is likely that these things have come upon you because your faults are past counting. …

He did not name sin first and then wickedness. Rather, he looked at wickedness as the bad state of the soul, and after that at the sins committed from that bad state, which he said are sins past counting. …

“And your sins are past counting” (Job 22:5). Eliphaz supposes this about Job. He knew that he was rich, and he says: You took pledges from your brothers as though they owed you, when they did not. For that is what “you took pledges for nothing” means. “You took pledges from your brothers for nothing” (Job 22:6). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Taking a pledge for nothing means exacting payment where nothing is owed and stripping the one-tunic poor man.
comments.comment:
“You took pledges from your brothers for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing” (Job 22:6). Let us take heed, we who lend at interest, that we never take pledges for nothing. … Eliphaz suspects this of Job because he knew he was rich, and he suspected that he had grown rich from some such sources. So he says, “You took pledges for nothing,” that is, when nothing was owed you. … But if I bring a false charge against a man, saying that he owes me when he cannot repay, and I demand and take, then I take a pledge for nothing. …

But if someone has one tunic, and on the pretext of demanding what is mine I strip that tunic off him, without pity for that naked man, I have taken away the clothing of the naked. … Often our debtor is poor beyond measure and cannot repay; and we shut up our hearts and become pitiless and cruel, not seeing that he feeds a wife and children and barely feeds himself on the few obols he earns. We demand payment bitterly, sometimes even when we have more than enough laid by.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what taking pledges for nothing and stripping the naked means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Failing to do good makes one answerable, especially taking the last morsel and sending widows and orphans away empty.
comments.comment:
“You did not even give water to the thirsty to drink, but you robbed the hungry of a morsel” (Job 22:7). … So not only doing wrong but also failing to do good makes a person answerable. All these are charges, and truly blameworthy things. But they were not true of Job, and they were not rightly said about him. …

Such things happen when debts are bitterly demanded. Sometimes a man has a single morsel and nothing more; even though he does not have a whole loaf, we take it from him, saying: But you owe. …

“And you sent widows away empty” (Job 22:9). Let us take care that, if a widow comes into our house, we never send her away empty. Let each of us, as far as he is able, fill the widow's lap with what he has. “And you ill-treated orphans” (Job 22:9). … No one ought to be ill-treated, but orphans above all must be spared. … More than other people, the poor, widows and orphans need help.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Both withholding easy kindness like water and judging by faces to please the powerful bring one to account.
comments.comment:
“You did not give water to the thirsty to drink, but deprived the hungry of a morsel. You admired the face of some, and you lodged those who are on the ground. You sent widows away empty, and you ill-treated orphans” (Job 22:7-9). So not only doing wrong but also failing to do good is liable to account. And he points out how far we ought to extend our kindness, since not giving drink to the thirsty is liable to account. Just as we receive a reward for the cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42), so he condemns Job for great harshness, as one who did not give even water, a kindness that costs nothing, and, the greater evil, to someone thirsty. …

“You admired the face of some.” That is, you also gave your judgements not justly, nor without passion, but to please men, for you became a respecter of persons. … “And you lodged those who are on the ground.” … meaning: you took away even the very bedding of the poor, so that they had to sleep on the floor, with nothing spread beneath them … “You sent widows away.” Either you stripped them of what they had, or rather, when they came to you asking for alms, you gave them nothing but sent them away without anything from you … “You ill-treated orphans.” To ill-treat orphans and the helpless is the mark of the utmost wickedness. … More than other people, the poor, widows and orphans need help.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what failing to do good means verse by verse in clear terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Snares are calamities that ensnare the soul, darkness is the loss of possessions and health, and covering waters show one overcome while asleep in sin.
comments.comment:
“Therefore snares have surrounded you” (Job 22:10). He calls snares the things that have befallen him, into which he has fallen, and by which his soul too is ensnared, through what has befallen him. …

“Your light has turned to darkness” (Job 22:11). You were in the light when you had your possessions, when your children were alive, when your body was healthy. But now you have gone down, as it were, into darkness, into these straits. … That is, in a desolate place, under the open sky, a wanderer, an exile, without a hearth. …

“And while you slept, water covered you” (Job 22:11). The words “while you slept, water covered you” mean this: the opposing power covered you, since you were not awake, since you did not sleep. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the images of snares, darkness and covering water.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The God who dwells on high sees all, brings down insolence, and can judge even through thick darkness.
comments.comment:
“Does not he who dwells on high look upon all?” (Job 22:12). But you think that God, who dwells on high, does not see what is done. As one who looks upon all things, then, he brings down those whose minds are puffed up by a habit of insolence. … It is likely, then, that since you too treated widows and orphans with insolence and took pledges from your brothers for nothing, this is why you have suffered these things and been brought low. …

“And you said: What has the Mighty One known?” (Job 22:13). … “Or will he judge through the thick darkness?” (Job 22:13). … God is able to judge even when he is in a storm. …

“And he goes about the circle of heaven” (Job 22:14). The providence of God goes the whole way round.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse stresses God's seeing and judging.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The righteous tread the everlasting path of providence and keep advancing even when seized before their time.
comments.comment:
“Will you keep watch on the everlasting path?” (Job 22:15). Can you really keep watch on the everlasting path along which the providence of God travels? “Which righteous men have trodden” (Job 22:15). … Righteous men have trodden the everlasting path. For they walk along an everlasting path, since everything lies before them to do so that they may attain the age to come. So even if they seem to walk just as others do, their soul itself still sets foot on everlasting paths. …

“Who were seized before their time” (Job 22:16). The righteous have often died before their time. For the righteous man, made perfect in a short while, fulfilled long years; for his soul is virtue in the Lord. “Their foundations are an overflowing river” (Job 22:16). … The foundations of the righteous are of that kind. They are always making progress, always growing in good things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the everlasting path and early death in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The houses filled with good things are the ruling part of the soul filled with virtues.
comments.comment: “And who filled their houses with good things” (Job 22:18). … He filled the houses of the righteous with good things. I do not take this to mean these houses of ours; rather he filled their houses, those of the ruling part of the soul, with good things. What good things? Self-control, justice, courage, prudence…
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ungodly plan apart from God, and the righteous scorn it.
comments.comment: “And the counsel of the ungodly is far from him. The righteous saw it and laughed” (Job 22:18-19). What the ungodly plan is far from God. The righteous, seeing the counsel of the ungodly, laughed them to scorn.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two verses plainly in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blameless sneer at wicked doctrines contrary to truth, and fire devours what the ungodly leave behind.
comments.comment:
“But the blameless man sneered at them” (Job 22:19). At whom? Or is it at the counsel of the ungodly? For example: people want to teach someone things that are contrary to the truth, by what they say, holding wicked doctrines as they do. When the blameless man sees these things, he sneers at them. …

“And fire will devour what is left of them” (Job 22:20). … Whatever has been left behind among the ungodly, once the earlier ones have died, the fire will devour.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Receive God's declaration by confessing sins and taking up his words from the heart.
comments.comment: “And receive a declaration from his mouth” (Job 22:22). I kept asking myself what “declaration” means. And in another edition I found “confession” in its place. So he is really saying: Confess your sins; receive from the mouth of God a declaration together with confession, and take up his words out of your heart. Eliphaz said this to admonish Job, as he supposed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Declaration means confession of sins or receiving God's law and words into the heart.
comments.comment: “Receive a declaration from his mouth, and take up his words in your heart” (Job 22:22). I was asking myself what “declaration” means, and I found that in another edition, that of Symmachus, “confession” stands in its place, and in Aquila “law.” So according to the one he says: Confess your sins, and be taught by God the manner of the declaration. According to the other: Receive law from God, and take his words into your heart. If you are righteous and worthy, let God dictate to you, and receive divine words in your heart, as Jeremiah later heard: “Behold, I have given my words into your mouth” (Jeremiah 1:9). … Or: Declare the sins you have committed, and from now on keep the words of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording about declaration in clear alternatives.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Turning, humbling oneself and confessing makes speech rich and renders one pure with God as helper.
comments.comment:
“But if you turn and humble yourself before the Lord” (Job 22:23). He admonishes him to turn, because he thinks Job has suffered these things for having sinned. …

“And like a rock of the torrent of Sophir” (Job 22:24). From the place where gold is produced it will come to you; that is, your speech will be rich and beautiful. …

“So the Almighty will be your helper against enemies” (Job 22:25): if you submit yourself, if you confess. … “And he will render you pure, like silver refined in the fire” (Job 22:25). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the call to turn and its promised outcome.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Gold should be thrown to the ground and treated as worthless.
comments.comment: “You will lay it on a mound in the rock, and like the rock of the torrent of Sophir” (Job 22:24). You will throw it to the ground and, as it were, ill-treat it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Turning and confessing brings free speech and light on one's ways, though Eliphaz spoke unjustly to innocent Job.
comments.comment:
“Then you will speak freely before the Lord” (Job 22:26). … If you humble yourself and endure what has befallen you, you will speak freely before the Lord. You will have freedom of speech, as one who has put away his sins. …

“There will be light upon your ways” (Job 22:28). … If you keep the admonition I give you, and turn, and confess. These things, then, were said to Job; but they were not said justly, for he had not sinned. If they are said to us, however, they are said justly. … “And he will restore to you a righteous way of life” (Job 22:28). To put it simply: he will give you back, he says, the whole settled state that suits a righteous life, so that your deeds are bright and glorious.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what free speech and light upon the ways promise.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job says his accuser and reproof lie close at hand, for God's heavy hand lies on him beyond anything he has done.
comments.comment:
“And indeed I know that the reproof comes from my own hand, and his hand has become heavy upon my groaning” (Job 23:2). That is: I carry my accuser about with me; the reproof, the proof of my evils, I have from my own house. I know, he says, that it is from what is at hand, that is, from the blow, and not from what I have done, that you think to bring your reproofs; for God has laid himself on me heavily, so that I groan.

I know, he says, that men's judgements come to them from their deeds; but the reproof has been laid on me beyond my strength, that is, apart from anything I have done.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job wished to plead his cause before God and learn His answer without charging Him with injustice, a wish fulfilled at the end of the book.
comments.comment:
“His hand has become heavy upon my groaning” (Job 23:2). If it were possible, he says, to have the verdict on these punishments given on the spot, I could find him. Would that I could go to law, he says, and meet him, and learn what he would say to me in reply to what I meant to say.

Do you see how he obtained the very thing he prayed for? For this is what happened at the end of the book. I wanted to learn, he says, what he would say to me, and whether he meant to go on punishing me in the same way. I said these things not as one who charges him with injustice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses mean in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even in great power, God deals with Job in truth rather than mere threats.
comments.comment: “And he will come against me in great strength; then he will not use threats against me” (Job 23:6). For even if he deals with me in great strength and threat, still I know that truth is with him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job prays for an end to his troubles, even through death, since “end” also means victory.
comments.comment:
“For truth and reproof are from him; and may he bring my judgement to its end” (Job 23:7). This was his prayer; this is what he means: that an end be set to my troubles. Then, he says: I wished these things to happen, so that I might die, not as though he were now about to judge.

Among the Hebrews, “end” and “victory” are expressed by one word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means and why it is worded as it is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job appeals to God’s knowledge of his eager obedience.
comments.comment: “For he already knows my way” (Job 23:10). He knows my way, he says, and that I have always been eager to obey …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though innocent, Job is dismayed because God may punish even where no sin gives Him right.
comments.comment: “Therefore I am dismayed before his face; I will consider, and I shall be terrified of him” (Job 23:15). I have not sinned, he says, and what of that? For God is free to punish not only by the right that sins give him; this too, I say, he may do without any sins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job’s unforeseen darkness is God’s blow on him alone, hence “before my face.”
comments.comment:
“For I did not know that darkness would come upon me, and before my face thick gloom covered me” (Job 23:17). This did not happen in the ordinary human course of things, he says: the evil was unforeseen, and I judge the blow to be from the hand of God.

And he rightly said “before my face,” for the darkness is not shared by all; it belongs to my own despondency.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse is worded as it is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ungodly gladly feed young men to carry out outrages through them.
comments.comment: “Their bread has become sweet to the young” (Job 24:5). The ungodly, he says, find it sweet to feed young men, so that they can carry out their outrages through them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God has not yet visited the oppressors, but He will examine and punish their offences.
comments.comment:
“But why has he himself made no visitation of these? They were on the earth, and they did not recognise it” (Job 24:12-13). That is: they despised everyone, they laughed at everyone; no one wrongs them or does them harm.

But he has not yet made a visitation of them, so he will do it afterwards: he will examine the offences they have committed and will not overlook them. Greedily they devoured orphans.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the delay in judgment in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowing means God has examined the wicked and handed them to darkness.
comments.comment: “And knowing their works, he handed them over to darkness” (Job 24:14). That is, having learned their works; or else, having examined them and put them to the test: that is what “knowing” means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though Job said he would appear righteous, he knew that no star is pure before God, as Paul did not justify himself.
comments.comment: For even if he said, 'I know that I will appear righteous,' yet he knew and is persuaded that, as a tester before God, 'there is no star pure in his sight' (Job 25:5) and he himself makes it clear. Such is what the blessed Paul says, writing: 'I do not know myself' (1 Corinthians 4:4). Then, not giving credit to himself, he proceeds: 'but not in this am I justified, but He who judges me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earth hangs on nothing because it is established on liquid, which has no hard and solid foundation.
comments.comment: What is said here is equal to what is said: 'He who made the earth stand upon the water,' and by Job: 'hanging the earth upon nothing' (Job 26:7); for if it is established in the sea, it does not have a hard and solid foundation, but in the waters it has the hanging. And every water has a ground beneath it. Since the sea has a ground beneath it, it must certainly have something underlying it. But nothing else is found except the liquid.
