For this reason, he says the earth is established upon the seas.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the earth can be 'hung upon nothing' and yet stand on the seas.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil tested Job through his goods, his body and his ill-timed friends to make him speak against Providence.
comments.comment:
“The Lord lives, who has judged me thus” (Job 27:2). The devil received authority over Job and examined him night and day: first through the things outside him, later through his very body, and after that through his friends as well. For when he had tried it through the wife and Job was not defeated, the devil brought on three friends. They were not enemies, nor did they hold treacherous doctrines; they spoke words of truth, but not well and not in season. And through these friends the devil planned to make Job utter something against Providence, to turn ungodly because of his toils, and to lose heart because of his pains.

… “And Job went on and said in his preamble” (Job 27:1): “The Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has embittered my soul” (Job 27:2), and so on. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job swears by the living Lord who judged that he should suffer and handed him over to testing.
comments.comment: … I swear to you, and I swear by the living Lord himself, who judged that I should suffer these things, the very one who handed me over to these straits, who gave the devil authority to have me tested and tortured with such trials. I swear by the Lord, and I say: “The Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has embittered my soul” (Job 27:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job's oath means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job resolves that nothing will turn him aside from his verdict.
comments.comment: “Nor will my soul meditate unjust things” (Job 27:4). That is: I will stand by the same verdict. No one will be able to turn me aside, no one to break in on me, no one to lead me away from what lies before me.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job will not accuse himself nor surrender his verdict even under pressure.
comments.comment: “Far be it from me to declare you righteous until I die, for I will not put away my innocence” (Job 27:5). That is: I will not accuse myself, nor change my ground, even if you say ten thousand things; I will not give up my verdict, even if you seem to have dropped your charge against me. Should I assent to what you say, that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would be declaring you righteous. I will not thrust away my innocence by thinking one thing about you and saying another.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job refuses to declare his hearers righteous for explaining his suffering and holds fast to righteousness with a clear conscience.
comments.comment:
“Far be it from me to declare you righteous until I die” (Job 27:5). If we were to agree with what you say, that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would have declared you righteous until I die.

“For I will not put away my innocence” (Job 27:5). I will not stop giving heed to righteousness; I will remember always to hold fast to it.

“For I am not conscious of having done anything out of place” (Job 27:6). His freedom of speech is great, both about his earlier life and about what he did in the time of his trouble, so that he can say: “I am not conscious of having done anything out of place.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses mean in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wrongdoer has no boldness to speak before God, but Job still speaks and answers back.
comments.comment:
“Or when distress comes upon him, has he any boldness before him?” (Job 27:9-10). What he says amounts to this: the one who does wrong, he says, has no boldness, neither to utter a sound nor to say the things that I am saying now; it has been taken from him and he has been muzzled.

But this has not happened to me: I speak, and I answer back. The unjust are not so.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses mean in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's order in nature shows his greater care for human affairs.
comments.comment: "For there is a place for silver," and so on (Job 28:1). He says this: the one who fixed an order in ordinary things has done so far more in human affairs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's providence orders all things, yet his governing of darkness remains untraceable and calls for trust rather than accusation.
comments.comment:
"For iron comes from the earth, and bronze is quarried like stone. He has set an order for darkness, and he himself searches out every limit" (Job 28:2-3). That is, he exercises providence and cares for affairs, and nothing passes by idly or at random.

Or rather, he is saying this: other things are plain, but God's dispensation cannot be traced and is unknown. … He said well, "He has set an order for darkness," showing that it knows how to give way and to withdraw altogether. Who drives away that gloom? Where does such good order come from in such a thing? Then he recounts his power, and then his wisdom, persuading one not to wish to call him to account.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verses as God's providence and his untraceable ordering of darkness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowledge grasps unchanging things, and understanding is discernment.
comments.comment: "But what is the place of knowledge?" (Job 28:12). Knowledge is the grasp in contemplation of things that always stay the same; understanding is discernment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom surpasses all silver, gold and precious stones in worth.
comments.comment: "And silver will not be weighed out in exchange for it" (Job 28:15). Nothing is worth as much as wisdom. If you take the silver and the gold in the simpler sense, Job will at once be saying that nothing is worthy of wisdom. … "With precious onyx and sapphire" (Job 28:16). Wisdom will not be compared even with precious onyx; no, nor will it be made equal to a sapphire.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses mean in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom should be drawn beyond all mighty, precious and hidden things.
comments.comment:
"Lofty things and gabis will not be mentioned" (Job 28:18). Neither lofty things nor gabis are worthy of wisdom. It seems to be set down of things that are mighty, as it were gigantic. But some say that "gabis" is the name for what stands up above the rim of a medimnus, which is called the heaped measure.

"And draw wisdom above the innermost things" (Job 28:18). The innermost things are those around India, or those in the country beyond it, where precious stones are found. That country yields these things to people, and among the rich they are thought marvellous. So beyond those innermost things, draw wisdom into yourself. Or else, "above the innermost things": the holy mysteries of God within, which are beyond all telling. Above all things, many as they are, draw wisdom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom is more excellent than precious stones, so nothing precious, not even the topaz of Ethiopia, equals it.
comments.comment: 'Your mouth's law is more precious to me than ten thousands of gold and silver' (Psalm 119:72), and 'Take instruction and do not forsake knowledge, which is tested above silver' (Prov 8:10); for wisdom is more excellent than precious stones, and every precious thing is not of equal value to it. Therefore it is also said to companions concerning it to Job: 'The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equaled to it' (Job 28:19).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom escapes every human being, even prophets and apostles.
comments.comment: "It has escaped every human being" (Job 28:21). It has escaped every human being, even if he is a prophet, even if he is an apostle.
comments.selected_reason: Plainly explains that wisdom is hidden from every human being, even prophets and apostles, in clear terms a general reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job recalls former prosperity to show God's providence.
comments.comment: "As when his lamp shone above my head, when by his light I walked in darkness" (Job 29:3). That he sought his former prosperity for this reason, so that God's providence might be shown, is clear from his saying, "When God guarded me" (Job 29:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job recalls former days in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job longs to show God's care by turning his means into virtue.
comments.comment:
"When God watched over my house" (Job 29:4). Symmachus: "When God fenced round my tent."

You see that this is what he longed for: to show God's oversight and providence. When I was young and had means, being righteous, he says, I made the material that served me into virtue, for I used everything well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what guarding the house means in daily conduct.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's virtues flowed out so that even the little ones were fed.
comments.comment:
"When my paths were flowing with butter" (Job 29:6). We have said before about the paths Job walked, that they were virtues. So his paths flowed with butter: he walked in self-control, and his self-control flowed out, as it were, so that many, even of the little ones, were fed by Job's self-control, by Job's righteousness, by his courage. That is the meaning of "When my paths were flowing with butter."

"And my mountains were flowing with milk" (Job 29:6). Whatever thoughts were high and great, these were Job's mountains, and he climbed up onto them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the butter and milk images in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job taught in the city for the common good.
comments.comment: "When I went out upright in the city" (Job 29:7). He gave his time to teaching and to doing good, out of love: not as a lover of himself, but as one who had a love that seeks the common good.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job sat early in the squares as a pattern of virtue.
comments.comment: "When I went out early into the city, and my seat was set in the squares" (Job 29:7). For like a ruler and teacher of virtue, he did not give his time to sleep and drinking, but out of love sat at daybreak in the squares, becoming a law and a pattern to those in the city.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what sitting in the squares means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hearers kept silence, feeling unworthy to speak beside Job's greater works.
comments.comment:
"Laying a finger on their mouth" (Job 29:9). It will seem that "laying a finger on their mouth" is a sign of silence.

But perhaps, since the hand is taken for works, as we have often shown, it shows that they laid their work on their mouth: they perceived, being slight in work, that they were not worthy to speak while Job was present, who had done greater works.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hearers blessed Job but could not follow the depth of his wisdom.
comments.comment:
"And those who heard me called me blessed" (Job 29:10).

From the same: So great was he, when he was not yet being tormented, that those who heard him called him blessed and wondered how he could understand and grasp so many things and was able to help those who heard him.

"For their tongue stuck to their throat" (Job 29:10). The tongue of those who heard me, and who called me blessed for what I said, stuck to their throat.

"For the ear heard and called me blessed" (Job 29:11).

From the same: It is written of Moses that he was afraid to look upon God because of the surpassing greatness of his brightness (Exodus 3:6). In the same way one might understand that Job's progress in wisdom was so surpassing that those who heard him could not look into the brilliance of his thoughts; and because they could not, they turned their eyes aside, unable to follow the great depth of his mind. That is why he says: "But the eye that saw me turned aside" (Job 29:11). Aquila and Symmachus have rendered it "It bore witness about me"; others, "But the eye that saw turned aside," meaning: I am not strong enough to speak against him.

…
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blessing of the perishing is great for finding life.
comments.comment:
"He who loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 10:39). For one who perishes in this way, according to the Saviour's word, and finds his life, the prayer and the blessing is a great thing.

Anyone of sound mind would pray that it might come upon him, and would wisely say: "The blessing," and so on (Job 29:13).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job guided blind minds and led lame conduct by his word.
comments.comment:
"I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame" (Job 29:15). As to the mind, he opened blind understandings and helped those maimed in soul, and he himself became their eye.

To those lamed in the steps of the soul he gave feet; by his word he became their foot and led both by the hand. The eye stands for guidance of the understanding, the foot for guidance of conduct.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the eye and foot images.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job gave feet to the lame and teaches fair judging between brothers.
comments.comment:
"And a foot to the lame" (Job 29:15). He himself gave steps even to those who were lamed, feet for the soul; and by his word he himself became their foot.

"And a cause I did not know, I searched out" (Job 29:16). He teaches us how we ought to judge, if we are ever called to arbitrate between brothers, so as to settle their affairs.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job protected the powerless even to danger in another's fight.
comments.comment:
"I was a father of the powerless" (Job 29:16). These words show the voice of one who helps the powerless, the weak.

"And a cause that I did not know, I searched out" (Job 29:16). You see his protection: it did not stop at money, nor at food and clothing; I stood forward even to the point of danger in another man's fight.
comments.selected_reason: Explains fatherly protection and searching out causes.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job set right seized matters, as Christ crushed opposing powers.
comments.comment:
"And I broke the molars of the unjust" (Job 29:17). See how hard the thing was: he says that he set the matter right even when it had already been seized.

Truly Christ, when he came, crushed the molars of the opposing powers. "The Lord has broken the molars of the lions" (Psalm 58:6), and it is written in the prophet: "From the midst of their teeth I snatched the prey" (Job 29:17).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job speaks of providence, not boasting, to explain where he stands.
comments.comment: "And I said: My age will grow old like the stem of a palm" (Job 29:18). See after how long a time he says this: not boasting or thinking great things of himself, but compelled to speak of God's providence, of the things in which he enjoyed it and of where he stands now.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's contempt means discerning the mockers' worthlessness rather than practising scorn.
comments.comment: “But now the least have laughed at me; now they admonish me in their turn, whose fathers I set at nought” (Job 30:1). Not that he made a practice of contempt, but that he knew them clearly, as the prophet said: “Every evildoer is set at nought before him” (Psalm 15:4). For he counted such people as nothing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job means by setting their fathers at nought.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The mockers remained barren of good, never bringing anything to completion despite want and escape.
comments.comment:
“And the strength of their hands, what is it to me? Over them the full end has perished. In want and famine he is barren, those who yesterday fled from waterless distress and misery” (Job 30:2-3).

From Olympiodorus and Origen: I did not even ask them for any help, he says, that they should use such words against me on that account. They had long owed a penalty, being wicked, and in a way the punishment flew away from them. Or else: they longed for death because of their extreme poverty and did not obtain it, and not even their want brought them to their senses so as to become begetters of good; they remained barren, those who only yesterday, a little while ago, had escaped from the desert and their misfortunes.

He seems to disparage them as low-born, from obscure villages and poor fathers. “Over them the full end has perished”: that is, they never brought anything good to completion.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The mockers forage mallows and roots in echoing woods and ravines to ease their hunger.
comments.comment:
“Those who go round the mallows on an echoing place, whose food was mallows” (Job 30:4). Mallow is a plant, they say, that quickly fills the one who eats it. “On an echoing place”: that is, on ravines and rocky ground, for such places ring and give back the voices of those who speak. Or he calls echoing the wooded place where the breath of the winds stirs the trees and makes a sound.

So he says that these men roamed the woods and the ravines and the places where running waters sound and babble; in their great want they searched out plants and scraped the roots of trees for food, as some comfort in their hunger.

“Dishonoured and despised, in want of every good thing” (Job 30:4). It is another wickedness to be like this even in poverty.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the mallows and the echoing place mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job is forbidden, not weak, to lay hands on himself.
comments.comment: “For would that I could lay hands on myself” (Job 30:24). You see that he says “if I could” not because of weakness but because he was forbidden.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job was not without fellow-feeling, yet he gave thanks when his children died.
comments.comment: Was Job's heart made of adamant? Were his inward parts fashioned from stone? Ten children fell to him in a brief moment of time, crushed by a single blow in the house of celebration, at the hour of enjoyment, when the devil brought the building down upon them. He saw a table mingled with blood; he saw children born at different times but reaching the end of life together. He did not wail, he did not tear his hair, he did not utter any ignoble sound, but he spoke that famous thanksgiving celebrated by all: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord" (Job 1:21). Was the man without fellow-feeling? How could that be, when he says of himself, "I wept for everyone who was afflicted" (Job 30:25)? But was he lying when he said this? Indeed, the truth bears witness for him that along with his other virtues he was also truthful. For it says, "A man blameless, righteous, God-fearing, truthful" (Job 1:1).
comments.selected_reason: Shows from Job's life that he felt for others yet gave thanks to God.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Excess of suffering removes shame at crying out in assembly.
comments.comment: “And I have stood in the assembly crying out” (Job 30:28). Because of the excess of his sufferings he is not ashamed even of the crowd of the gathering.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job was not ashamed to cry out in the assembly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Affliction has made him wild like the birds, forgetting his own nature.
comments.comment: “I have become a brother of sirens and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). I have fallen, he says, into the wildness of the birds; I have forgotten my own nature, and I am in no better state than they.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what becoming a brother of sirens and ostriches means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job could not literally have cared for orphans from the womb, so his good practice began with the word fulfilled in him.
comments.comment: Job says: “And even if I have eaten my morsel alone and have not shared with the orphan, except as a father guided them from the womb of my mother” (Job 31:17-18); for how was he able to provide for and care for orphans from the womb of a mother? Thus, therefore, I take it: a praiseworthy practice is a continuous progression; then the practice takes its beginning when the word is fulfilled. I am able, therefore, to say this: he says that I have done good things not after the evil things, but the word having been fulfilled in me, it began from the praiseworthy things; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His servants wanted to share his life because he had been kind to them.
comments.comment: "And if my maidservants often said, 'Who would grant us to be filled with his flesh?', for I was very kind" (Job 31:31). That is, to enjoy his life, because I was sweet to them.
comments.selected_reason: Clarifies what the maidservants' saying means in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He lodged strangers indoors and supplied provisions, not only giving them shelter.
comments.comment: "No stranger lodged outside, and my door was open to everyone who came" (Job 31:32). For he did not only care for them by taking them in, but also supplied them with provisions against the poverty that would follow.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's hospitality beyond merely opening his door.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He fell silent so his friends could speak, while calling God as witness.
comments.comment: "And Job ceased from words" (Job 31:40). Job fell silent, giving them room to speak; but he took note, called God as witness and called down curses on himself, because his friends had been silenced.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His timely silence was praiseworthy, though his heart never ceased understanding divine things.
comments.comment: "And Job ceased from his words" (Job 31:40). "And his three friends also held their peace and no longer answered Job, for Job was righteous before them" (Job 32:1). He did not simply cease. His heart, which understood divine things, did not cease. For there is a time for every matter under heaven (Ecclesiastes 3:1): "a time to keep silent and a time to speak" (Ecclesiastes 3:7). So when it was the time to answer the three, he spoke; when it was the time, after he had stopped their mouths, he fell silent. And I think the words "Job ceased" are said in his praise.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's silence as deliberate and praiseworthy rather than mere inactivity.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Elihu held back from declaring his knowledge of suffering and the prosperity of the unjust in this life alone, yet youth can also speak wisely when God teaches.
comments.comment:
“Therefore I held my peace, afraid to declare my own knowledge to you” (Job 32:6). He has knowledge of how human beings suffer, of why human beings fall into certain straits if one looks at this life alone, and of how many prosper though they are unjust. I saw people doing wrong and breaking the law, and my feet were almost shaken. If I look into this life alone, my steps were all but poured away (Psalm 73:2).

“It is not the long-lived who are wise” (Job 32:9). For it does not follow, he says, that only old men are wise; it is possible to hear something noble from youth too. For if time makes people wise, God does so much more.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom comes with time only to the one who desires and pursues it, so an old man is not wise by necessity.
comments.comment: Furthermore, those who think that learnings are by nature are rebuked by this; for nothing that belongs to human essence by nature and necessity is perfected by time. No mortal, as a living being, adds to himself by time; but the wise man is attained by time. "For when I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I reasoned as a child; when I have become a man, I laid aside the things of a child" (1 Cor 13:11). To this, someone might oppose the "not those of many years are wise, nor the elders know judgment" (Job 32:9), contrary to what was said by Job to those who think otherwise. Yet both can be understood as following one another; for the blessed Job says that he who begins wisdom and hastens to take it up will not take it up as it happens, but will take it up in much time. But neither would Elihu say contrary to this; for if someone did not desire wisdom, but had progressed in age, he would already be wise; for the old man is not wise by necessity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Elihu addresses the friends because their refutation of Job was inadequate before they fell silent.
comments.comment: “For I will speak while you listen, until you have examined the words, and I will attend to you” (Job 32:11-12). Either he is saying this: even when you were refuting, you did not refute as you should have; or that afterwards you fell silent. That is how it bears on “For I will speak while you listen.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Elihu intervenes, observing that the friends failed to refute Job adequately before falling silent.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul that loves learning conceives and shapes its words like a child brought to term, finding relief when speaking to an understanding hearer.
comments.comment:
“For the spirit of my belly is destroying me” (Job 32:18). Just as a woman becomes pregnant, and when the child being born in her has been formed, she comes to her labor pains until she gives birth to what she had conceived before: think with me that something of this kind happens in the soul of the one who loves learning too. It conceives the word, and as it is being declared it shapes it and stamps it with order. And when, after stamping and shaping it, the word has become ready, it hands it over not as an unready and unfinished miscarriage, but, I would say, as something brought to term and made complete.

“And my belly is like a skin of new wine, fermenting and tied up” (Job 32:19). It seems to me that the saying in the Gospel was spoken from this place: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Mark 2:22).

“I will speak so that I may find rest, when I have opened my lips” (Job 32:20). A man who meets with an understanding hearer, and is full of words, finds rest in speaking, and says: “I will speak so that I may find rest.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains Elihu's urgency to speak through the vivid imagery of pregnancy, fermenting wine, and finding rest before an understanding hearer.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Elihu refuses to flatter mortal persons or fear their opinion, lest he be consumed like those who show partiality.
comments.comment:
“For I do not know how to admire a face” (Job 32:22). I do not have this skill, of admiring a person's face. No, I despise human beings, and the shame that mortals can bring, and the respect that they command.

“Otherwise the moths will devour me too” (Job 32:22). As though the moths eat through those who show partiality to the faces of men.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's words about the divine Spirit and the breath of the Almighty show the Holy Spirit as fellow-creator with God, not as one of God's creatures.
comments.comment:
… So we are permitted to know from what these have declared. Job: "A divine Spirit made me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me" (Job 33:4). David, in the hundred and fourth Psalm: "You will send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you will renew the face of the earth" (Psalm 104:30). The apostle confirms this, writing to the Corinthians the second time: "So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new" (2 Corinthians 5:17). And in the thirty-third Psalm: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers" (Psalm 33:6).

Do not run past what can be heard straight from these words. See rather that the Spirit of God, as creator and good God, abiding for ever, supplies the creation with a lasting friendship, has bound it fast with bonds that cannot be loosed, and has set it firm. Unshaken, he also upholds all things by his own power. See too that it is unlawful to call a creature him who creates and gives strength to the creatures of God.
comments.selected_reason: Links Job 33:4 directly to the claim that the Spirit creates and sustains, which clarifies what Job means by Spirit and breath in that verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Elihu misread Job as claiming to be more righteous than God, when Job only insisted on his integrity without accusing God of injustice.
comments.comment: "For how do you say, 'I am righteous, and he has not heard me'?" (Job 33:12). What then happened? He did not think this. Elihu supposed it, but Job did not speak with any such mind, that he was more righteous than God; he meant that he had done these things, and yet he did not charge God with injustice. Elihu supposed this. But he rightly charged those others, who had betrayed God's side and denied it.
comments.selected_reason: Clarifies what Elihu is rebuking at this point in the dialogue and how it differs from what Job actually held.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One ought to yield to God's glory even without fully knowing Him, rather than insist on learning everything.
comments.comment: “He who did not feel shame before the face of one held in honour, nor knows how to pay honour to the great” (Job 34:19). For even if you do not know, you still ought to yield much to him and to his glory, so as not to seek to learn everything.
comments.selected_reason: Clarifies Elihu's point about reverence toward God who shows no partiality.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Good and evil lie with us now, but not in the age to come.
comments.comment: “For he will no longer lay it upon a man” (Job 34:23). He seems to be saying this: now the good and the bad lie with us, but in the age to come no longer.
comments.selected_reason: Offers a plain reading of what Elihu means by God not laying judgment on man as He does now.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Elihu does not demand Job's agreement as a debt owed to him, but invites Job to speak and argue for himself.
comments.comment:
“For as for the one who says to the Mighty One, ‘I have received; I will not take a pledge; apart from myself I shall see; you show me’” (Job 34:31-32). Some have interpreted it thus: no one dares to say to one who is stronger, “You have taken what is mine unjustly, not by way of a pledge, as though it were owed to you, and you have taken it against my will; show that you have done this with good reason.” But if no one dares to say these things to a man of power, how, he says, can you be so bold as to say such things against God?

Symmachus rendered it thus: “Since I have taken up speech towards God, I will not hold back; unhindered, you make it plain to me.” His meaning is this: since I have taken up speech on God's behalf, says Elihu, I do not hold back, but go on with the argument unhindered. And if I do not speak well, you make it plain, that is, refute the argument.

But I think rather that the text should be understood thus: it is not that, because I have chosen to speak on God's behalf, you must for that reason simply agree with me as well, as though I were demanding payment of a debt. “Apart from myself I shall see; you show me” means: apart from my own argument I want to know whether you have anything to say in reply. I keep silence so that you may speak; take up the argument, if you can.
comments.selected_reason: Walks through competing readings of Elihu's challenge and settles on one a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only those free from love of the world look up to heaven.
comments.comment: “Look up to heaven” (Job 35:5). No lover of the world looks up to heaven. Let us not love the world, nor the things in the world (1 John 2:15). If we love the things here, we do not look up to heaven.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Human sin does not harm God, nor does righteousness benefit Him.
comments.comment:
“If you have sinned, what will you do?” (Job 35:6). That is, you will not wrong him; but neither will you benefit him if you are righteous.

For since he was saying, “If I have sinned, what can I do?” (Job 7:20), “What shall I do?” he says, this is in order to say: Why? Does he care about your sinning because he is wronged? As though he suffered harm?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sinner should come to the high priest for forgiveness, since righteousness adds nothing to God.
comments.comment:
“If you have sinned, what will you do?” (Job 35:6). If you look up to heaven and consider the clouds, you will understand how you have sinned. What must you do? Come to the high priest and beg the high priest to offer a sacrifice for you. For “if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1-2).

“And if you have done much lawlessness, what can you do?” (Job 35:6). You will do this great thing: you will undo your many lawless deeds. That is why, for the incurable ills that we cannot heal in ourselves, Jesus Christ came from heaven, so that he might heal what is incurable and the word might come true: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1).

“Well then, since you are righteous, what will you give him?” (Job 35:7). But if you are righteous before God, what do you have to give in keeping with your righteousness? And if you are righteous, as you say, what will you add to him?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: This present age is night, with full light kept for the future.
comments.comment:
“He who appoints the night watches” (Job 35:10). He goes through the praises of God, his commendations and his hymns. The one who appoints the night watches is God himself. I want to see how God is the one who appoints the night watches.

This whole age is night; it is darkness. The light is being kept for you. The light you see now, you see through a mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12). And “in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9): one day we are going to see it.

So the whole age is night; and since it is night, there are many wars, and many wild beasts prowl about.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God posts guards, the angels, to watch over those in the night of this life.
comments.comment: “He who appoints night watches” (Job 35:10). … Since, then, the affairs in the darkness of this life are night, there is need of guards posted for this night, so that the guards, those set over the nights, may keep watch over those who are in the night, and may come and guard us from the robbers. Who, then, are the guards posted by God in the night watches? “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Psalm 34:7). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the night watches as angelic guards in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sinner remains unseparated from senseless beasts.
comments.comment: “He who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth” (Job 35:11). If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth. For “man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them” (Psalm 49:20). If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth; rather, it is said to you: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 32:9). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only the Creator knows the earth's measures, and its exact size and varied lands show purposeful design.
comments.comment:
“Who fixed its measures, if you know? Or who is it that stretched a line over it?” (Job 38:5). The Greeks did want to say something about the measure of the earth: the diameter of the earth, they say, is twenty-five myriads of stades. But the passage seems to show that the measure of the earth is beyond everyone's grasp; only the Saviour knows it, who is also the Creator.

He said “measures,” and not “measure,” to set before us the differences in the earth. What is the measure of this or that land: of the East, say, which bears the spices? What is the measure of the land that bears pepper, or the animals? For not everything grows everywhere.

These measures, then, are with the Word of God. So the earth has not come to be of this size without reason, nor by chance; it seems to me that if even the slightest thing were added, it would be out of place, and if anything were taken away, by the same reasoning it would spoil the whole earth. This is what the measures and the line hint at.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plural measures and why the earth's size is purposeful.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The earth stands firmly fixed by God's will, while the cornerstone can also be understood as the Son who joins Jews and Gentiles in himself.
comments.comment:
“And who is it that laid a cornerstone upon it?” (Job 38:6). Who is it that laid a cornerstone upon it, so that it stands so firmly fixed, as though built upon the secure footing of a foundation? By the will of God, for in his hand are all the ends of the earth (Psalm 95:4).

“A cornerstone”: this can also be understood of the only-begotten Son of God, made flesh for our sake, according to the word in the Psalms: “The stone which they rejected has become the head of the corner” (Psalm 118:22). For coming to earth by the good pleasure of the Father, he joined in himself the two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles, just as, of course, the cornerstone binds both walls together.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what holds the earth firm and why it is called a cornerstone.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God marked out the land when it lay hidden in the deeps and set it apart by bars and gates on the waters.
comments.comment: [Of the earth:] For He marked it out; that is, when of old it lay hidden in the deeps, invisible and unformed (Genesis 1:2), He made it visible and finished. He marked it out, for, as the books of Moses attest, He said: “Let the water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:9). So it appeared out of the waters; and though it was under water and wholly unworked, He set it apart by itself, placing bars and gates on the deeps (compare Job 38:10) and separating it thoroughly from the waters.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God set bars and gates on the waters when the dry land appeared.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God holds the raging sea within bounds by a mere word, so its turmoil proclaims God's strength.
comments.comment:
“And I said to it, ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond’” (Job 38:11). Symmachus: “Up to here let the swelling of your waves be set.” So securely does he hold it in, as if with bars; and so easily, as if by a set order. For “I said,” he says, and there is no answering back, when this comes about with no constraint driving it, and that although great force and strength are lashing the sea.

This is why he did not let it be calm or gentle: so that it might proclaim God's strength, its nature fighting against the command and the command everywhere prevailing.

If the water were gentle, many would have credited its good order to the nature of water. But as it is, troubled, lashed, driven back within, and unable to pass its bounds, by its very turmoil it proclaims the strength of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sea is violent yet bounded.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God takes pride in making man from earth, since to make a rational creature of clay goes beyond all wonder.
comments.comment: Then how is it that God takes pride in the making of man? For He says somewhere to the blessed Job, “Did you take clay of the earth and form a living creature, and set it on the earth endowed with speech?” (Job 38:14). For to make a rational living creature out of earth would, I think, go beyond all wonder.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Raven chicks are reared not by their parents but by God, who feeds them as the Gospel says.
comments.comment: “And who prepared food for the raven?” (Job 38:41). For it is said not to rear its young. The grown birds, naturally, being large, find food for themselves; but who rears the young? Is it not the word of God? As the Gospel too says: “The birds of the heaven do not sow, nor do they reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Flesh-eating birds like the vulture possess a natural wisdom directed toward war and the dead.
comments.comment: “Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up, and the vulture, having settled on its nest, lodges on a jutting rock and in a hidden place?” (Job 39:27-28). … If among the flesh-eaters there is some reasoning wisdom, present in each from the knowledge it has by nature, and directed to knowing, for one of them war, for others the dead, you see it in the vulture too, a single bird borne through the air.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job gives up his case at once, seeing he has no answer before such a master.
comments.comment:
… “Why am I still judged, being admonished and reproving the Lord, when I hear such things, I who am nothing?” (Job 40:4). “Why am I still judged?” he says, by way of a preface; and from the start he gave up the first place. I am beaten in my case before you, he says; why do you press the suit further? For what answer can be given?

And how should one look such a master in the face? I, he says, kept on seeking the cause of the blow that fell on me; but I brought no charge against the work of creation, and I have nothing to say against what has been said. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's answer in 40:4 in terms a general reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Freedom to answer God is a prize for endurance, given only when the loins are girded.
comments.comment:
… “No; but gird your loins like a man” (Job 40:7). I give you freedom of speech: I will ask you, and you answer me. God is already giving him a prize. He questions a man, in that he inquires of him, in that he gives him the right to answer. Had he not conquered, he would not have received this; had he not endured, he would not have heard: “Gird your loins like a man; I will ask you, and you answer me.”

… Let no one answer God before he has become a man and girded his loins like a man. For as long as his loins are not girded, but slack, not bound round or drawn tight, he cannot fittingly answer the Lord. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what girding the loins means for answering God in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God gives Job freedom to answer because His just claims are abundant.
comments.comment:
… “But gird your loins like a man; I will ask you, and you answer me” (Job 40:7). For those who are confident in an abundance of just claims do not even shun their opponents but give them leave, so that the victory may come out of that abundance.

Then he also makes his defence to him: I care about human beings; it is plain from this why I brought this trial upon you. I give you freedom to speak: I will ask you, and you answer me. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God already pledges future rewards by speaking through the whirlwind and granting speech.
comments.comment:
… “I will ask you, and you answer me” (Job 40:7). The full rewards of the contests are stored up, after this life, for those who have fought well. Yet even now, no less, the grace of God gives the athletes a pledge. That is why, when Job had fought the greatest fights; when he had lost his possessions and glorified the one who had given them; when he had put his children from him and given thanks to the one who had taken them; when he saw that he was, as it were, bringing up worms from his body and was not overcome by his pains: then God gives him the first-fruits and the pledge that belong to athletes, speaking to him through whirlwind and clouds.

So when he had heard the earlier words, though he ought to have answered God, he keeps silent, as one who has no freedom to answer him. For he did not yet know what Moses wrote later, that “Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice” (Exodus 19:19). Not knowing this, then, he does not want to answer God. But God gives him freedom to speak.

… So great is the kindness of God that he takes on the role not of one who judges, but of one who goes to judgment with the man. And many Scriptures have taught this: “Come, and let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:18). And: “My people” (or rather, God will argue his case with the people), “my people, what have I done to you, or how have I wearied you? Answer me” (Micah 6:3), and so on. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nothing befalls us apart from God's judgment, which lets hidden endurance and courage shine.
comments.comment:
… “Do not reject my judgment” (Job 40:8). Do not reject this judgment of mine. Let us keep this saying in mind as a useful one. Whenever God judges that we should suffer something, should lose a child, should lose a ruler, should fall ill in body, should endure any one of these things whatever: none of these can happen to us unless God judges it. For not even a sparrow falls into a snare without the will of the Father in heaven (Matthew 10:29). Since, then, none of these things happens apart from God's judgment, it is said to the one who suffers: “Do not reject my judgment”: do not deny that I have judged concerning you.

“Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?” (Job 40:8). I am making my defense to you. You were righteous, but you were not seen to be. You had endurance; I had to give an occasion for your endurance to shine. You had courage, but it lay hidden in you; the toils that came upon you showed your courage.

… Let us remember these things in times of trouble, and let us think that we hear God present and saying to us: “Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?” Let us not be shown to be unrighteous, or ungodly. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains suffering as under God's judgment and showing righteousness in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The same hardships are lashes to the sinner but contests to the righteous, as happened to Job.
comments.comment: For many are the lashes of the sinner; and it has been said to us in other places that the same circumstances are lashes to the sinners, but contests to the righteous. Never do the burdensome and evil things come upon the pious as a scourge, but as a testing, just as it happened to Job, that the righteous might be revealed (Job 40:8).
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes the scourge of the sinner from the testing of the righteous, as in Job.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one afflicted in everything who endures to the end is proven righteous, as Job was.
comments.comment: … for the heart of everyone who endures in obscurity is tested, and he who is afflicted in everything is not distressed, but enduring until the end, he is proven righteous; such as Job, to whom God said: 'If perhaps I may prove you, you shall be more righteous than I' (Job 40:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God says these things not to condemn Job but to display the righteousness he already has.
comments.comment: … “Do you think that I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?” (Job 40:8). He means the present divine answer: I do not say these things to condemn you, he says, but to show you righteous. Or he is speaking of the trial, calling the permission a divine dealing, that is: that I had ordained this to happen for some other reason. He did not say, “that you might become,” but, “that you might appear as what you were,” so that you might teach the others. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The command to put on glory shows Job's lowliness by setting God's greatness before him.
comments.comment: … “Take up now loftiness and power, and clothe yourself in glory and honour” (Job 40:10). Crown yourself: put on glory, put on honour, put on comeliness. The insolent one made war on you, but you humbled the proud one and turned his ranks back far away in shame. … So it is not for display; or else it is for all the other things as well, or even for the knowledge of God. See how far he convicts Job of the lowliness of his nature: he does not say that you are lowly, but that I am great, and that he cannot do what I can. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because Job conquered his assailant, he is charged to humble every insolent and proud one.
comments.comment:
… “Take on, then, loftiness and power” (Job 40:10). Crown yourself; clothe yourself with glory, clothe yourself with honor.

“And send out angels in wrath, and humble every insolent one” (Job 40:11). “And quench the proud” (Job 40:12). The insolent one made war against you. The insolent one once said to me: “Put forth your hand.” He said to me: “Touch all that he has.” He said to me about you that you would surely bless me to my face (Job 1:11). But you have conquered all the same. That is why I say to you: Take courage; humble every insolent one, and humble his angels. That one became proud against you; but you, quench the proud. That one is ungodly against you; but you, strike down the ungodly at once.

“And fill their faces with dishonor” (Job 40:13). Convict sinners by showing them to be sinners. Fill their faces with dishonor through the conviction that is in you. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wild beasts beside Job are the opposing powers placed under human authority.
comments.comment: … “But look, there are wild beasts beside you; it eats grass like oxen” (Job 40:15). The wild beasts are the opposing powers, about which the Prophet prayed, saying: “Do not hand over to the wild beasts the soul that confesses to you” (Psalm 74:19). The wild beasts are the opposing powers over which you, O man, have received authority. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The beasts stand beside every victor.
comments.comment: … “But see, there are wild beasts beside you” (Job 40:15). … Beside you, Job; beside everyone who is mindful; beside everyone who has won the victory. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The beasts beside Job are the opposing powers, made manifest because they lacked strength against his virtue.
comments.comment: Regarding Job, it is said: 'Behold, beasts eat grass beside you like oxen' (Job 40:15), not that the immediate beasts were driven wild in nature by Job, but that the disorder of opposing powers was being made manifest because they lacked strength against the greatness of the saint's virtue. And many things are found in the Scripture where animals are mystically led.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The grass-eating means the worms that came out of Job and ate him.
comments.comment: … “He eats grass just like oxen” (Job 40:15). He means the worms, the ones that came out of Job himself and were eating him up. For “an end,” he says, “my hand by you”; and see, it eats him up like grass. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job the athlete learns his dragon-opponent is tamed for all who endure.
comments.comment: … “But now, behold, wild beasts are with you” (Job 40:15). As an athlete, learn about the dragon, your opponent. With you, then, he says, and with everyone who endures, these beasts are tamed and made subject. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dragon's first attack makes the man a fornicator.
comments.comment: … “And his power is on the navel of his belly” (Job 40:16). This is the first power set against the man. It is from here that it begins to make him a fornicator. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Through desire the dragon overpowers both male and female, the loin standing for the man and the navel for the woman.
comments.comment: For especially through this desire he is able both to overturn and to wrestle down human beings — the loin being understood, as of the man, and the navel of the belly decently as of the woman — so that it may be shown that through such desire he most of all overpowers both the male and the female (Job 40:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, like a fisherman, puts his flesh on the hook of his divinity as bait, so that the devil seizes it and is drawn up.
comments.comment: [Christ speaks:] I am a fisherman fishing for fish. For just as a fisherman puts a worm on the hook, extends the rod, and sometimes lets the hook sink down and sometimes pulls and drags it, so that by making the worm appear to flee he prepares the fish to rush upon it—so I too, placing my body on the hook of my divinity like a worm—for I am a worm and not a man (Psalm 22:6)—sometimes I pull death in as if in fear, and sometimes I let the hook sink down as if taking courage, so that the devil, like a fish leaping upon the worm—that is, coming against the flesh—may without knowing it fall upon the hook of the divinity, and having fallen may be dragged up, so that what was said by Job may be fulfilled in him: You will draw the dragon with a hook (Job 41:1).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the early writers read the hook that draws up the dragon.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Job cannot do what the Only-begotten later accomplished in catching the dragon with the bait of his flesh.
comments.comment: “Will you lead a dragon with a hook, and put a halter round his nose?” (Job 41:1). Can you, then, he says, O Job, do what the Only-begotten later accomplished? For he held out his own flesh to him as a kind of bait, and through his own nails, as through hooks, he caught the fish Leviathan. That is what the Hebrew has, and it means the dragon.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each wicked person takes a share of the dragon, whose extremities no one can kill without the power of God watching over him.
comments.comment:
“And nations of Phoenicians divide it up” (Job 41:6). Since the Canaanites, who are also the Phoenicians, are charged with great wickedness, that is why he says, “And nations of Phoenicians will divide him up.” Each one takes some part of the dragon, if by race he is a Canaanite and a Phoenician.

“And if every ship came together, they could not carry a single hide of his tail” (Job 41:7). The last parts of the dragon, his very extremities, all the ships together cannot put to death. Human beings, who use their bodies as ships, cannot carry a single hide of his tail. By themselves, on their own, they cannot. But when divine power watches over us, we are able to carry not only a single hide of his tail but the whole of him, and to put the whole of him to death. And each of us puts the devil to death, as far as it lies with himself, in keeping with what is said by the Apostle: “And may God crush Satan under your feet soon” (Romans 16:20).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one can bind the savage beast by his own strength, for the Lord alone won that war through the cross once for all.
comments.comment:
“Will you lay a hand on him, remembering the war that is waged in his body? And let it happen no more” (Job 41:8). By war he means here the turmoil, the savagery, his onrush. How can that be done? he says. Such is the beast: savage and powerful and senseless. Can you, he says, bind him down by your own strength? Or even so much as remember and conceive the war that is to be waged in his body?

By his body he means the demons, since he is their head; and this war the Lord won through the trophy of the cross. And “let it happen no more” is said because the cross has taken place once; for “he who died to sin,” it says, “died once for all” (Romans 6:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the war in his body means and why it happens no more.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dragon hides his own face and deceives with many masks, taking a virtuous face for each vice.
comments.comment:
… these actors on the stage: sometimes the masks of governors, sometimes of other kings, sometimes of women. Their own face is hidden, and what they are does not show; what they seem to be is what people see. The dragon is like that. He never shows his own face; but if he has taken on a face to deceive people, that is the one he uses. And this enemy certainly has many masks, and for each vice he takes on a face of virtue.

And a little later, on what follows, the rest of the verse written above: The face he has put on, who is able to expose it? Who is able to uncover it and show what the dragon is within? Such too are certain others, his disciples, “who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7:15).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil once deceived many by appearing as what he was not, until Christ exposed his illusion.
comments.comment: Long ago the enemy was great in his scheming against human beings, and by his illusions he deceived many, and the detection of his deceit was difficult—so that the Spirit says about him: “Who will uncover the face of his garment?” (Job 41:13) and so on. For he did not appear as what he was, but he produced an illusion of himself corresponding to whatever he was scheming. Therefore many were deceived by him. But when the Savior came, then all his illusion was exposed. For the things he did of old that went unrecognized are now known by the grace of Christ, and the things by which he once deceived human beings are now trampled underfoot by them. For faith is stronger than every assault of the devil and madness of demons.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'uncover the face of his garment' says about the devil's deceit before Christ.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His face cannot be found, for lifting it by word or thought uncovers something worse, and he is folded up everywhere.
comments.comment: He is a person, imitating the deceptive Protagonist; for he does not have a face that is entirely ordered. Thus he says in Job: 'Who will strip off his face-covering?' (Job 41:13). You cannot say that this is his face. If you lift his face by word or by thought, something worse is found. Furthermore, he is folded up everywhere; 'into the folding of his armor' no one can enter. And if you enter, it is folded up again.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The many outward masks rise from unseen wickedness folded up in the thoughts of his heart.
comments.comment:
… I ran back to the memory of the sacred writings set down in this God-inspired book of Job, where, as in a bodily figure, he sketches what is exceedingly formless and many-sided and hidden in the schemes, and in the shedding of the outward masks, of the devil, the author of evil, and of the wicked demons. For it says: “Who will uncover the face of his garment?” (Job 41:13).

And since the roots of this variety that shows on the outside rise up as from some depth of unseen wickedness, these words too are added to what has been said: “Who will uncover the face of his garment?” That is: who is able to enter into the thoughts of his heart, since they are folded up together?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nothing in the dragon is simple, for he is crafty and folded, and only a holy person can expose the fold.
comments.comment:
“And who could get inside the fold of his breastplate?” (Job 41:13). Do you see? This is called a breastplate, and a chest; and the breastplate is where the ruling faculty is. His breastplate is not simple. He has nothing simple about him. He is crafty; he is folded over. So who could get inside the fold of his breastplate? A saint can expose him and show that his breastplate is folded over; but the saint's own breastplate is not folded.

“Who will open the gates of his face?” (Job 41:14). He hides the things stored up within. So who will open the gates of his face? Who is the one able to expose him and to show how much deceit, how much venom, how many evils he keeps stored up?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fear around the dragon’s teeth is not the fear of God.
comments.comment: “Around his teeth is fear” (Job 41:14). Of these teeth it is said, “You have broken the teeth of sinners” (Psalm 3:7), and, “The Lord will crush the molars of the lions” (Psalm 58:6). This fear is not the fear of God; it is the fear that is around his teeth. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Everything inside the dragon is hard asp venom.
comments.comment: “His insides are bronze asps” (Job 41:15). These are his teachings, his hidden thoughts. Everything is the venom of asps, everything that is inside him. And they are not some soft asps but hard ones; for the asps are hard.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dragon’s mouth is the place from which destroying words come, so we keep watch not to be burned.
comments.comment:
“From his mouth” (Job 41:19): the blasphemies and the words of ungodly and godless teachers.

“From his mouth go out burning torches, and braziers of fire are flung about” (Job 41:19). I think, for my part, that all the ungodly who bring in godless doctrines would properly be members of the dragon. … The dragon's mouth may also be something understood figuratively, and with it the place from which the destroying words come. … If I ever heard a speech that accused the Creator under the pretext of Christianity, a speech, say, championing the teachings of Marcion …; when they speak ill of the Maker of heaven and earth, when they say that he is not, and is not of spiritual substance either, the sort of things these men say: you will see that from the mouth of such people burning torches go out and braziers of fire are flung about. That is why we, who know this, should keep watch over ourselves, so that those torches never burn us and the braziers of fire never touch us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture says glued, not united, for with him what seems one is many.
comments.comment: “And the pieces of flesh of his body are glued together” (Job 41:23). He could have said, “The pieces of flesh of his body are united.” But he did not say it, for they are not united; that is not so. With him, the one is many; or else things that seem to be one are glued together, as the one who says “are glued,” not “are united,” shows.
comments.selected_reason: Plainly explains why the flakes of flesh are called glued rather than united in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dragon’s heart is hard and unyielding, while the one who follows the Word yields like gold to receive God’s imprint.
comments.comment: “His heart is set fast like a stone; it stands like an anvil that cannot be beaten out” (Job 41:24). He is not beaten out, he does not follow the word; by his own nature he is hard, not to be beaten out, unyielding. And if anyone has drawn power from the devil, from this dragon, he too has the heart that cannot be beaten out and is not beaten out. But if someone is gold, he follows the Word, the goldsmith; and so he yields, until he becomes a leaf of gold and receives the impressions of the letters of God, in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory for ever. Amen.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the stone heart and the gold that yields in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job received double because he showed double virtue, while Christ promises a hundredfold.
comments.comment:
“And the Lord gave double, as much as Job had before, doubling it” (Job 42:10). The noble athlete who underwent every trial, Job, most courageous of men, receives the prizes of his endurance, as the Scripture says: everything double compared with what he had before.

But the Lord Jesus Christ gives prizes not double but a hundredfold. For he says: “Whoever leaves father or mother, house, brothers, sisters, for my sake or for the sake of the Gospel,” as is written in the Gospel according to Mark, “will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life” (Mark 10:29-30). He would not have received double of what he had before if he had not shown double the virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse gives double and what it means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job, after patience had won, recovered his body and double his goods, and he waited for his children to be restored.
comments.comment: And so that workman of God's victory, having blunted every dart of temptation with the breastplate and shield of patience, soon recovered the wholeness of his body from God, and possessed double what he had lost (Job 42:10). And if he had wished his children also to be restored, he could have been called father again. But he preferred to have them returned to him on that day; he postponed such great joy, confident in the Lord. He endured a voluntary childlessness for a time, so that he would not live without some patience.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's patience in the restoring of his goods and his children.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: The livestock were lost and so were doubled, but the children only died, so God gives the same number again to make double in the resurrection.
comments.comment:
… Look at the livestock: he had, it says, fourteen thousand sheep, for at the beginning he had seven thousand (Job 1:3); six thousand camels, for at the beginning he had three thousand; a thousand yoke of oxen, for at first there were five hundred. The same holds for the grazing asses. Yet seven sons and three daughters, it says, are born to him, as many as there were before (Job 1:2). But there ought to have been fourteen sons and six daughters, so that they would be double the children he lost.

We say, then, that the sheep and the livestock were lost, but the sons and the daughters died; they were not lost. So God gave him as many children again, so that in the resurrection he would have them double; and so God has made him the father of twice as many children as he was father of before.

But if the soul were extinguished after death, and the resurrection were not real, he would have had to be given fourteen sons and six daughters. That is why Scripture has reverently kept to the statement that he received seven sons. For if fourteen sons and six daughters had been born to him, with the teaching on the resurrection still standing, the children given to him would not be double but triple what they were at first.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse doubles the livestock but not the children in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “After the stroke” counts from when suffering began, fitting a doubling of the years of former prosperity.
comments.comment:
“And Job lived after the stroke a hundred and seventy years, and all the years he lived were two hundred and forty” (Job 42:16). How is Job understood to have lived a hundred and seventy years after the stroke, when the whole of his life came to two hundred and forty-eight years?

We say, then, reckoning closely, that since he received all his goods back double, if he also received back double the years of his former prosperity, this is how the count should be made. He lived seventy-seven years in his former plenty, and from the time he received the stroke he remained in suffering fourteen years. So “after the stroke” must be understood to mean not from when the stroke ceased but from when it began. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's years were repaid double like his goods, making two hundred and forty-eight years in all.
comments.comment:
… he lived another hundred and fifty-six years. For since the years of his former prosperity were seventy-eight, the double time of his later good fortune comes to a hundred and fifty-six years; and when the fourteen years of the stroke are added before them, the total is a hundred and seventy years. So he is found to have lived a hundred and seventy years after the stroke, that is, from the time the stroke was brought on him, as Scripture says. In this way the double repayment of his plenty is also kept.

To sum up, then, you will count like this: he lived in wealth and in the blessing of children seventy-eight years; in the loss of everything and the affliction of his body, fourteen years; in his second good fortune, a hundred and fifty-six years; so that the whole time of his life is two hundred and forty-eight years, as the sacred book about him says.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The added line that Job will rise again is missing from Aquila and Symmachus but kept by Theodotion and the Seventy, and is accepted as received from the fathers.
comments.comment:
“And Job died, old and full of days” (Job 42:17). “And it is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up.” Aquila and Symmachus, on reaching this point, ended the book, since they follow the Hebrew; but Theodotion ends it together with the Seventy, leaving nothing out, neither the time nor the life.

It is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up: the righteous, clearly. For “the ungodly,” it says, “will not rise in judgement, nor sinners in the council of the righteous” (Psalm 1:5).

We accept these words too, even if not as belonging to the whole fabric of the book, yet as if one of the saints had woven them into it; still, we accept all of it, since we have received the book in this form from the fathers. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
